rows.title: Clinical trial of a targeted chemotherapy drug delivered by a catheter to treat dogs with glioma brain tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Dogs and humans are the only species in which primary brain tumors are common. In dogs, a type of malignant tumor called a glioma accounts for approximately 35% of all spontaneous primary brain tumors. Even with treatment, the prognosis for both dogs and humans with gliomas is poor, and there is no cure. Current therapies such as radiation aim at extending quantity and improving quality of life. In this clinical trial, we are testing the safety and effectiveness of molecularly targeted cytotoxins, which are chemotherapeutic drugs, delivered directly to the patient's brain tumor. Developed by researchers at the Thomas K. Hearn Brain Tumor Research Centerat the Wake Forest School of Medicine, the unique chemotherapeutic drugs used in this trial are designed to affect only cancerous cells, and not normal brain tissue. Earlier generations of these molecularly targeted cyotoxins have been used safely and effectively in dogs with gliomas. Using specialized catheters the cytotoxins are infused directly into the tumor over a several hour period. The drug treatment is monitored continuously with MRI to allow the neurosurgeon to precisely track the drug delivery.

**As a dog owner, how can I participate in this trial? ** If you suspect that your dog may have a brain tumor, you should arrange for an appointment with your local veterinarian. They will perform a complete neurological examination, which is the first and fundamental step in establishing a diagnosis in animals with brain disease. It is also a prerequisite for them to determine which additional diagnostic tests to recommend. However, advanced imaging studies of the brain, such as MRI, interpreted in conjunction with the neurological examination and other supporting tests, are usually necessary to best characterize diseases of the brain. If your local veterinarian cannot perform an MRI, they will often refer you to a veterinary neurologist who offers this service. Our Neurology and Neurosurgery Service works on a referral only basis, which means that your local veterinarian must first evaluate your pet and arrange for an appointment to see one of our specialists. In order to be eligible for this specific clinical trial, your dog must have an MRI of the brain that demonstrates an abnormality consistent with a glioma.

Clinical Trial Inclusion Criteria: - Dogs of any age, breed, or sex between 3-45 kg in body weight - Clinical signs of mild to moderate neurologic dysfunction referable to the brain - MRI evidence of a single telencephalic intra-axial mass lesion consistent with a glioma - No clinical or other diagnostic evidence of other significant systemic disease. - Dogs must have gross, measurable disease (> 1cm in diameter) on a current MRI

We are happy to evaluate clinical and imaging findings to determine patient eligibility for this clinical trial.

To expedite this process, please complete and return our Neurology Clinical Trial Consultation Form: https://virginiatech.qualtrics.com/SE/?SID=SV_2ct6Cm6EegrTga1.

rows.title: Clinical trial for dogs newly diagnosed with osteosarcoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
In this study we will investigate the therapeutic potential of immune cells known as invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells, made from the blood of a healthy donor dog, in dogs with bone cancer. iNKT cells are potent immune cells that have been shown to kill cancer cells in mouse models and in some human cancer patients. The iNKT cells directly kill the tumor (cancer cell) and  they also boost the patient's own anti-tumor (cancer-killing) immune responses. In this study, we will genetically modify these natural killer T cells (NKT) cells to express a protein known as a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). The CAR directs the genetically modified CAR-iNKT cells to a target protein (known as B7H3) on the bone cancer cell. The CAR-iNKT cells kill the bone cancer cells and activate the immune system to do the same. The purpose of this study is to determine i) the safety of CAR-iNKT cells, ii) their ability to traffic to the bone tumor in your dog’s leg and exert an anti-cancer effect there, iii) their ability to delay or prevent metastatic disease and iv) how long the CAR-iNKT cells remain in your dog’s body. 


This clinical trial is fully funded and at no cost to owners. Covered procedures include:

  1. Bloodwork for general health screening
  2. Chest radiographs to be sure the osteosarcoma has not spread to the lungs prior to treatment
  3. Bone biopsy to confirm osteosarcoma and the presence of the B7H3 target protein
  4. Cellular therapy with iNKT cells
  5. Amputation of the affected limb (~10 days after cell therapy) and all post-op care/hospitalization
  6. Standard of care chemotherapy
  7. Follow up monitoring of bloodwork and chest radiographs


All clinical trial visits are in person at the University of Pennsylvania School of Veterinary Medicine in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

rows.title: Feasibility and dose-optimization clinical trial of local immunotherapy for solid tumors in canine cancer patients
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
WHY IS THIS STUDY BEING DONE?

Immunotherapies are a class of anti-cancer treatments that work by activating a patient’s own immune system to fight specific diseases, including cancer. A number of immunotherapies have been approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in humans in a wide range of diseases, including cancer. While these therapies have shown positive results in cancers of blood cells, they have had more limited successes in solid tumors like soft tissue sarcoma. This is thought to be in part because it is hard to get enough of the drug into the tumor when it is given through the blood stream (intravenously) without causing serious side effects. To overcome this limitation, this research study will use injections of immunotherapies directly through the skin into the tumor (intra-tumoral injections). 


The primary goal of this research study is to test whether it is safe and feasible to treat tumors by injecting them with a certain type of immunotherapy called T-cell engagers (TCEs).  A T cell is a special kind of white blood cell that attacks sick cells in your body, including virus-infected cells and cancer cells. TCEs are a new kind of cancer immunotherapy that helps a patient’s own T cells find and kill cancer cells. They work like a connector: one end sticks to a cancer cell, and the other end sticks to a T cell. By pulling the two cells together, the TCE helps the T cell recognize the cancer cell and activate its killing response. In this research study, two different TCEs will be tested together (TCE combination). They work in much the same way, but each one attaches to different markers on cancer cells and T cells. Because they target different markers, the two treatments can help T cells kill cancer cells more effectively, even at lower doses of each TCE, which helps reduce the chance of harmful side effects. The goal is to make the therapy work better while still keeping patients safe.


The study will test different doses of TCEs per injection, different numbers of injections placed into the tumor itself, and the product used to dilute the TCEs. The TCE combination will be diluted either in sterile saline (a solution of salt and water) or in hydrogel (a water-based gel). The hydrogel’s job is to slowly release the drugs into the tumor, with the goal to keep the cancer cells exposed to the drugs for a longer time. This may help the treatment work better and could also reduce side effects. The TCE combination will also be mixed with sterile fluorescent dye(s) that will help researchers track where the injections were placed in the tumor. The fluorescent dye(s) have already been used in multiple canine and human clinical trials with no known side effects.  


The “investigational” part of the study are the intratumoral injections of the TCE combinations diluted in sterile saline or hydrogel. These TCEs are investigational drugs, which means they have not yet been approved by the FDA or the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) for use in dogs or other species. The purpose of this study is to test the safety and the biological effect of the TCE combination in canine patients with soft tissue sarcoma (STS), rather than to specifically provide medical treatment to the enrolled patient.

rows.title: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.

rows.title: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

rows.title: Using nanoparticles to deliver anti-tumor genes to pet dogs with high-grade gliomas
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Gliomas are among the most common and most aggressive primary brain tumors in pet dogs. Established definitive treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, or a combination of these treatments. Surgical resection alone does not improve survival times achieved with supportive care alone, and is therefore not recommended. Radiation therapy provides an average of 14 months of survival time. The purpose of this study is to investigate a novel treatment option with the goal being to improve outcomes for dogs with high grade gliomas. Treatment in this study consists of injections of nanoparticles (NPs) that target brain tumor cells and result in their death.


This is a single site, prospective, three arm clinical trial with no control (placebo) group. Each patient will be randomly assigned into one of these three groups. The treatment arms are:


1) surgical resection + nanoparticle administration

2) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy

3) surgical resection + stereotactic radiation therapy + nanoparticle administration

rows.title: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.


IACUC: 24619

Study number: VCCT-26-014


The study will provide $3000 toward initial diagnotic tests or radiation therapy for your pet.

rows.title: Using MRI to differentiate between benign and cancerous lymph nodes in dogs with head and neck cancer
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records

Purpose To assess the ability of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to differentiate between benign and metastatic (cancerous) lymph nodes Background Current methods of diagnosing and staging head and neck neoplasia (cancer) in dogs are invasive, and the biopsy samples required to determine if the cancer has spread to surrounding lymph nodes can be difficult to obtain. This study aims to characterize the appearance of regional lymph nodes using diffusion weighted MR sequences in a group of canine patients with confirmed head or neck neoplasia, and evaluate the ability of these sequences to differentiate non-metastatic from metastatic lymph nodes. If successful, this method could provide a non-invasive diagnostic option that does not utilize ionizing radiation. Such a method of lymph node characterization could prove useful in the staging of tumors, leading to improved prediction of expected outcome and appropriate treatment recommendations. rows.title: AuroLase Therapy for the Treatment of Solid Tumors in Cats and Dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: AuroLase Therapy uses a therapeutic medical device designed to selectively destroy solid tumors using near infrared illumination from a laser. AuroLase Therapy is comprised of three components: 1) an off-the-shelf near infrared laser source, 2) an off-the-shelf interstitial fiber optic probe for delivery of the laser energy to a site near or inside the tumor, and 3) the investigational gold nanoparticles (AuroShell particles), a near infrared absorbing, physiologically inert material designed to absorb and convert laser energy into heat. Intravenously administered AuroShell particles have previously shown efficacy and high selectivity over surrounding healthy tissues in a variety of animal models. Human clinical trials are now progressing utilizing AuroLase Therapy for a number of clinical presentations and tumor types such as refractory head and neck, prostate, lung, and brain cancers. The purpose of the proposed study is to evaluate this therapy in dogs and cats with easily accessible spontaneous tumors. Dogs and cats will receive one AuroLase Therapy treatment and will then be followed for one month after treatment to observe anticancer activity and side effects. Dogs or cats that have been diagnosed with a malignant tumor that is easily accessible will be eligible for this study. Required study visits include pretreatment, day 0 (which may be the same day as pretreatment), day 1, 14, and 28. A physical examination and a small blood sample will be collected pretreatment, and days 1, 14, and 28. The AuroShell particles will be administered intravenously on study day 0. On study day 1 (approximately 24 hours after AuroShell particle infusion), your pet will be anesthetized for approximately 30 minutes for application of the laser treatment. While under anesthesia a tumor biopsy will be performed. Tumor biopsies will be repeated on study day 14 and 28 under mild sedation. Your pet may experience some local pain at the site of the biopsy and laser application. If this occurs, the clinician will prescribe pain medication. After study day 28 (or sooner if your pet is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional follow-up and treatment options with you. The study will cover all costs related to AuroLase Therapy treatment and required recheck examinations, blood tests and tumor biopsies. In addition, a gift of $250.00 will be applied as a credit to your UW Veterinary Care account.

rows.description: Lymphoma is a common cancer in dogs, and is routinely treated with combination chemotherapy protocols. One of the drugs in this protocol, vincristine, can occasionally cause side effects such as nausea and vomiting, especially due to ileus, where the normal motility of the gut is decreased. For such patients, vinblastine is often substituted in the chemotherapy protocol. Most oncologists feel this drug has effectiveness against lymphoma; however, the true effectiveness of vinblastine in treating lymphoma has not been established. This study will establish how many patients do respond to this drug, justifying vinblastine's use in lymphoma protocols. Dogs must have a diagnosis of untreated lymphoma, determined by cytology or histopathology, have a lymph node a minimum of 2 cm for assessment, and not carry a specific mutation that causes abnormal pumping of drug out of the cell (MDR1). rows.description: 1. Purpose of the project The primary objective of the study is to evaluate whether needle biopsy of retropharyngeal lymph nodes (those in the very back of the throat behind the nose) are valuable staging tests for dogs with head and neck tumors. 2. Eligibility for participation Dogs will be eligible to participate in the study if the presence of a head, neck or nasal tumor is confirmed via cytology or histopathology prior to the initiation of therapy and if they are undergoing advanced imaging (CT scan) of their tumor with evaluation of the lymph nodes for therapeutic planning as part of their normal diagnostic plan. 3. Description of procedure Dogs will receive a CT scan, as part of their standard diagnostic or therapeutic work up, before participating in this procedure. The area under their chin will be shaved and cleanly prepped with alcohol. Using ultrasound guidance, a needle attached to a syringe will be placed through the skin and into the retropharyngeal lymph node. A sample of cells will be removed by applying suction and spread on a slide for review. There are two retropharyngeal lymph nodes and both will be sampled. rows.title: Stereotactic Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Nasal Tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Nasal tumors are locally aggressive tumors of the nasal passages. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for dogs affected by this cancer. At the UW-VMTH, we have a TomoTherapy radiation delivery system, which targets radiation to the tumor while sparing the surrounding normal tissues from side effects. Stereotactic radiotherapy (SRT) is the use of this very precise technology to deliver high doses of radiation in fewer treatments compared to conventional protocols. A conventional radiation protocol for nasal tumors involves 10 radiation treatments, given as one treatment per day for 10 days. To take advantage of the extreme accuracy of stereotactic radiation therapy, we are investigating the efficacy of a shorter protocol in which only 3 treatments are delivered over one week (on Monday, Wednesday and Friday). Compared to the conventional protocol, a higher dose of radiation is used for each treatment to achieve a similarly effective total dose. Potential benefits of stereotactic radiation therapy include fewer visits to the hospital for radiation treatments, fewer anesthetic events, and a lower risk of short-term side effects. We will assess the safety of this new approach by monitoring for any radiation-induced changes in the eye. Our hypothesis is that by delivering stereotactic radiation therapy, we will safely decrease the number of treatments needed to effectively treat nasal tumors in dogs. Dogs with a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis of cancer affecting the nasal cavity (carcinoma or sarcoma), stages I-III may be eligible to participate in this study. Dogs with cribriform plate involvement and/or metastasis, or previous treatment for this cancer are not eligible. Dogs will be evaluated at 2 & 4 weeks and 3 & 6 months post-radiotherapy to assess tumor response and side effects, including ocular changes. Clients will receive financial compensation to cover the cost of their dog's follow-up evaluations, including scheduled hospital visits for a full examination including eye exams and a post-treatment CT scan.

rows.title: Endoscopic/Laparoscopic Treatment of Inoperable Cancer With a Targeted Endoscopic Electroporation System (EES)-Now available in th
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Work at the Cork Cancer Research Center in Ireland has lead to the development of a novel new energy based therapy for treating inoperable human cancers including those unresponsive to conventional chemo and radiotherapy. Since 2004 over 400 energy focused cancer treatments have been provided to patients with unresponsive skin based cancers at the Mercy University Hospital, Cork. Over 85% of the tumors treated have been reduced in size by more than 50% after one treatment. The treatment involves the application of a brief electrical pulse (under local anesthetic in people) directly to the tumor tissue. This causes the tumor cells to become temporarily porous and results in a significant increase in the tumor cells absorption of the chemotherapeutic drug. This treatment is extremely suitable for animals particularly in cases where the cancer is considered inoperable. In animals, the device is attached to an existing endoscope and during a standard endoscopic procedure the tumor is enveloped (sometimes in several locations due to tumor size) and treated after IV administration of chemotherapy with the intent that circulating chemotherapy will drive into the open cancer cells, effectively killing them. For intra-operative locations, the device may be placed directly onto the tumor with surgical access if necessary. A newer device is now available to treat tumors using thoracoscopy or laparoscopy as minimally invasive options. Tumors that may respond include colon tumors, stomach, esophageal, prostate, adrenal and other non-resectable cancers. Frequently Asked Questions: 1) Will this therapy cure the cancer? The therapy is effective at the location where the electrodes are placed on the animal i.e. the visible tumor mass; provided contact can be made endoscopically the tumor mass can be reduced if not eliminated with minimal side effects 2) How long does the treatment take? The procedure is completed under anesthesia (isoflurane/sevoflurane). Injection of a low dose of chemotherapy (the total is 5% of what would be used conventionally) and application of electrodes directly to the tumor with pulses used taking less than 1/10th of a second to deliver. The pet is treated and able to go home the same day. 3) What chemotherapy drug is used? Is the chemotherapy toxic? The drug used in combination with the electric pulses is Bleomycin. On its own, bleomycin is very poorly absorbed by cells and is considered a poor drug for the treatment of cancer. However, by making the tumor cells porous (because they receive an electrical pulse), the drug can enter locally (but not to other cells in the body), and this results in the tumor cells dying. It also means that the toxicity is limited to the site of where the electrodes are placed which means side effects are truly unlikely. 4) Will my pet lose its hair from the chemo? No. A very low concentration of drug is used and is only toxic at the location the electrodes are placed i.e. on the tumor tissue. 5) Does anesthetic need to be used? Will my pet feel pain or discomfort? Human patients who receive local anesthetic feel the electric pulse and have described it as a dull thud. The anticipation is apparently worse than the discomfort of the pulse which it is important to point out subsides virtually immediately (the pulse lasts 1/10th of a second). In animals, the easiest solution is general anesthetic (isoflurane/sevoflurane) normally for between 15-30mins in total. In this case no discomfort is felt by the pet. 6) Is it an invasive treatment, does it involve surgery and stitches afterward? Unless surgery is needed to approach the tumor, no surgery is involved and therefore the therapy does not involve stitches. For extremely large tumors that are operable a possible combination treatment is to deliver the treatment to the healthy tissue margins afterward to minimize the risk of residual cancer cells escaping. 7) What side effects does the treatment have? No side effects have been reported from the drug or the electric pulses in humans. Some inflammation may occur in larger tumors but this can easily be managed with medication or with many cases subsides without additional therapy needed. 8) What should happen after treatment? How long will it take to see a response? The tumor is not surgically removed; it shrinks and regresses in size over a period of a few weeks after treatment. The speed at which this happens can vary depending on the type and size of the tumor. Normally a reduction in size can be seen within 2 weeks and regression can continue for up to 2 months. Aggressive cancers can be retreated after 4-6 weeks to improve the speed of regression. 9) Which patients are best for treatment? Any animal with a solid tumor can be treated. Dogs, Cats, and Horses have all been treated successfully. 10) Which cancers are best for treatment? Any solid tumor can be treated. Those located on the skin are the most straightforward to identify, diagnose and treat. Internal cancers can be treated during open surgery or via this specially designed endoscopic/internal equipment developed at the Cork Cancer Research Center. Particularly suited are those cancers considered inoperable or that involve invasive surgery e.g. to the head, legs or internal organs. rows.title: Clinical Trials for dogs with lymphoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: It is known that a specific protein in the membrane of the nucleus, XP01, controls the shuttling of several key proteins in and out of the nucleus (center) of the cell. Recent studies indicate that blocking XP01 can induce death of cancer cells as they cannot recover function when the shuttling of proteins is disrupted; in contrast, normal cells appear to be less sensitive to this effect, likely because they are not growing in an uncontrolled manner. The novel compound Verdinexor is an inhibitor of XP01 that is given orally twice per week. Verdinexor has been studied in 2 separate clinical trials in dogs with lymphoma with over 75 dogs treated to date. Approximately 30-40% of dogs with both newly diagnosed and relapsed lymphoma appear to benefit from Verdinexor treatment staying on therapy for over 8 weeks. The main side effect of Verdinexor is loss of appetite and weight loss, with other side effect such as intestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea) and liver value elevations occurring less frequently. RV1001 is a novel inhibitor of a cell protein called PI3K delta. This drug, like verdinexor, is given orally. PI3Kdelta has an important role in both T and B cells, providing signals for cell survival. Recently, RV1001 was evaluated in a clinical trial of dogs with both T and B cell lymphoma. The overall objective response rate was 62% (3 complete and 10 partial responses) demonstrating very high biologic activity. Increases in liver enzymes were the primary side effect observed, and this was prevented in most dogs by giving the drug Monday through Friday with the weekends off, rather than daily without a break. While the activity of RV1001 was very high, the average time on drug was only 4 weeks indicating that the dogs rapidly developed resistance. Given the potential for both RV1001 and verdinexor to have activity in dogs with lymphoma and the non-overlapping side effects of each drug, the purpose of this study is to evaluate the effects of both drugs in combination. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity when verdinexor is administered in combination with RV1001 in dogs with lymphoma, and to assess the clinical toxicities in dogs with lymphoma receiving verdinexor in combination with RV1001.

rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) is a chaperone protein that is important in maintenance of several proteins needed to promote cancer cell growth and survival. Hsp90 activity has been shown to be increased in cancer cells. Hsp90 inhibitor drug conjugates (HDCs) are small molecules that link an anti-cancer drug to an Hsp90 inhibitor. The Hsp90 inhibitor helps bring the anti-cancer drug inside the cancer cells. The anti-cancer drug can then be slowly released inside the cancer cells. Synta Pharmaceuticals has developed STA-12-8960, an Hsp90 inhibitor linked to SN-38, an active metabolite of the anti-cancer (chemotherapy) drug irinotecan. A recently completed clinical trial in dogs with cancer identified a dose of 15 mg/kg given intravenously weekly as the maximum tolerated dose. In this study, several responses to therapy were noted including dogs with lymphoma and mast cell tumors. Side effects were mild in most dogs and consisted of appetite loss and diarrhea, although these were well controlled with additional medications. Objective of the trial: The objective of this study is to compare the plasma and intratumoral concentrations of SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma receiving first irinotecan followed by STA-12-8960 to determine whether STA-12-8960 does result in greater intratumoral drug concentrations.

rows.description: Purpose of the study: Use a model (COXEN) to predict which of the standard chemotherapy protocols an individual dog's tumor is most sensitive to. Administer (post amputation) chemotherapy to the patient based on the predictions generated by the model. Determine if this gives better outcomes for those patients (longer survival). Primary Eligibility Criteria: Dogs with confirmed or suspected diagnosis of osteosarcoma of a limb, with no evidence of metastases (chest x-rays). Dogs must be free of other serious diseases (physical exam, blood tests). All dogs must have amputation as the treatment of the tumor, performed at CSU. They cannot have had any prior treatment for the tumor. Study Protocol: Initial screening tests (physical exam, blood and urine test, x-rays of the affected limb and chest). Surgery to amputate limb (tumor samples will be analyzed by COXEN method). Dogs will be assigned to chemotherapy based on the results of COXEN analysis with either single agent carboplatin, single agent doxorubicin, or alternating doxorubicin/carboplatin. Additional visits will be for blood tests, chemotherapy treatments, and intermittent chest x-rays. Owner Responsibilities: To make and keep all study related appointments. Financial responsibility is the owner's, aside from the points listed below. Financial Incentives: The study pays for the cost of the COXEN analysis to determine drug sensitivity of tumor and gives $1000 towards the cost of chemotherapy. The study pays for chest x-rays until the development of metastatic disease. All owners are responsible for what would be the costs of the single agent carboplatin protocol for their dog; the additional costs associated with single agent doxorubicin or alternating doxorubicin/carboplatin will be covered by the study. Owners are alsop responsible for all other costs associated with their dog's treatment and participation in this study.

rows.title: Lymph Node Mapping in dogs with Mast Cell Tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose of Study: Mast cell tumors are a very common skin tumor in dogs, and a common mechanism of spread in the body (metastasis) is to nearby lymph nodes. If tumor spread to lymph nodes is identified (as part of staging), this is important information that often influences treatment recommendations. Currently, standard protocols for looking for metastasis in lymph nodes most commonly include aspiration cytology. Aspiration cytology is minimally invasive, but may miss a diagnosis of lymph node metastasis in a concerning number of patients. Early literature suggests metastatic disease may be missed by lymph node aspiration in up to 40% of patients! The concern is that not only does aspiration cytology only sample a very small amount of a given lymph node, but that it is difficult to ensure that we have correctly predicted the optimal lymph node to sample for any given mast cell tumor. Lymph node mapping, a technique to visualize the lymphatic drainage of tumors by which tumor cells might spread, is increasingly used to improve cancer staging and treatment protocols in the treatment of cancer in humans. Efforts are made to identify the sentinel lymph node or primary lymph node that is most likely to demonstrate evidence of metastatic disease if it is present. This lymph node can then be surgically removed with the primary tumor, in order to be evaluated microscopically for spread of cancer. However the common method of sentinel lymph node mapping performed in people is not widely available to veterinarians. This trial is being performed to hopefully identify an alternative method of sentinel lymph node mapping that can be more widely accessible to a greater number of veterinary practitioners. By doing so, we hope that this will improve the accuracy of cancer diagnoses and treatment recommendations we make for dogs with mast cell tumors and other cancers, improving their quality of life and lifespan. Contact: Email Dr. Stephanie Majeski (smajeski@ucdavis.edu) or Dr. Michele Steffey (masteffey@ucdavis.edu) Call (530) 752-1393 to make an appointment Participation Requirements: Dogs must have been diagnosed with a peripheral mast cell tumor, have been evaluated by or received a consult from a clinician the Soft Tissue Surgery service to determine if LN mapping is viable for your individual dog, and you have elected surgical excision of this tumor both for diagnostic and treatment purposes. Initial Evaluation for Participation: Evaluation by the U.C. Davis V.M.T.H. Oncology or Soft Tissue Surgery services. Specific preoperative diagnostic tests to ensure that your pet is safe for surgical removal of the mast cell tumor will be recommended by the clinician that you consult with on these services. Procedures: If you choose to enroll your dog, lymph node mapping procedures will be performed the day before and the day of surgery. These will be discussed in more detail at the time of your appointment. Benefits: The study will cover costs associated with the sentinel lymph node mapping imaging. There is no charge to you for these procedures. Possible benefits of participating in this study for your dog include more sensitive identification of metastasis (spread of cancer) if it is present. If early metastasis is more sensitively identified, we can then make more accurate treatment recommendations for your pet. It is our hope that in addition to benefiting your dog, we will benefit future patients by advancing the standard of care offered when treating this type of cancer, improving care provided to larger numbers of veterinary cancer patients. Owner Responsibilities: If you allow your dog to participate in this study, you will be responsible for bringing your dog to the U.C. Davis V.M.T.H. for 1) preoperative evaluation of and 2) surgical removal of the mast cell tumor, and covering the standard costs associated with medical workup for and surgical removal of the mast cell tumor. If you are calling to schedule an appointment and already know that you are interested in having your dog participate in this study, please inform the coordinators so that they can make sure to schedule appropriately for the mapping procedures.

rows.title: Dasatinib Phase I Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics in Dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose of the study: To evaluate the safety, metabolism, and appropriate dosing of dasatinib in dogs. Dasatinib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Primary Eligibility Criteria: Dogs with a confirmed diagnosis of cancer that is > 2 cm in diameter and accessible for biopsy. 3 week washout from chemotherapy, 2 weeks from other tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. Palladia), 6 weeks from radiation therapy, 72 hours from antacids (Pepcid, Prilosec, Tums). Concurrent steroid therapy is allowed, but dogs must have been receiving steroids for at least three days (ideally a week) prior to the first therapeutic dose of dasatinib. Study Protocol: Oral dasatinib given once daily at home. First dose will be micro-dose which will be used to determine the therapeutic dose to be given. Recheck visits required on days 0, 7, & 14 and then every other week. Overnight hospitalization required on days 0, 7, and 14 of study for serial blood collections. Blood samples collected at every visit; tumor biopsies performed prior to first treatment and at day 14. Owner Responsibilities: Follow appointment schedule required by study protocol. Be comfortable administering oral medications. Costs of any ancillary medications given that are not related to side effects of the study drug. Financial Incentives: Study pays for all costs associated with trial. $750 credit to VTH account which can be used for future treatment after completion of the trial

rows.title: Oncolytic Poxvirus Therapy for Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Dogs Pilot Safety Study

rows.description: Purpose of the study: To determine if recombinant myxoma virus therapy is safe in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. There are several ongoing clinical trials testing the efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy in humans, but trials in canine cancer patients are extremely rare. Mouse models of canine cancers have been successfully treated with oncolytic viruses. Clinical trials using oncolytic virotherapy in dogs are the next step in the process of advancing treatment options for dogs with cancer. Primary Eligibility Criteria: Dogs with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of soft tissue sarcoma. Biopsy tissue must be available for analysis. Tumor must be at least 2 cm in diameter and accessible for biopsies. Prior surgery acceptable; 2 week washout from chemotherapy, 6 weeks from radiation therapy. Dogs living in household with an immunocompromised person or a rabbit will be ineligible. Study Protocol: Dogs will receive an injection of the poxvirus directly into the tumor Recheck visits are required 1, 4, 7, 14, & 28 days following virus injection for collection of blood, urine, feces, and saliva to monitor for adverse effects and virus shedding. Tumor biopsies will be performed on days 4 and 14 following virus injection. Study is completed at day 28 visit or earlier if there is evidence of tumor progression or significant adverse effects of virus injection. The first three dogs enrolled in this study will need to be hospitalized at CSU for 7 days following the virus injection. Owner Responsibilities: Cost of biopsy prior to starting treatment to confirm diagnosis. Follow appointment schedule required by study protocol. Complete owner diary daily including documentation of tumor size, weight of dog, and any side effects noted Financial Incentives: Study pays for all costs associated with trial. rows.title: Immunolight Therapy for Canine Cancer - Phase II (Solid Tumors & Lymphoma)
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study With the support of the Immunolight team, doctors in the department of Radiation Oncology at North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine are working with researchers at Duke University's School of Medicine to develop Immunolight Therapy as a treatment option for dogs with various tumors. The goal of this therapy is to provide an alternative treatment for cancer; the hallmark of Immunolight Therapyis a non-invasive, immune-based treatment that does not involve the introduction of cytotoxic agents used in conventional chemotherapy, thus eliminating the potentially life altering side effects of current therapies. Immunolight Therapy involves the use of psoralen, a naturally-occurring compound found in broccoli and figs, as well as phosphors, tiny particles that absorb energy from X-rays to emit UV light in and around cells. For decades, psoralen has been used to treat skin disorders, cancer and autoimmune disease. Immunolight Therapy converts penetrating forms of energy, such as low-dose radiation therapy, into energies that are capable of activating the drug inside the body. This activation generates light inside the tumor to induce an immune response against cancer akin to a related technology (photopheresis) that has been successfully used to treat people with lymphoma of the skin. Immunolight Therapy has shown great promise in laboratory models of human breast cancer. Its short term safety has been documented in dogs; in that safety study, Immunolight Therapy also showed great promise as treatment for some kinds of cancer. Enrolling dogs with: - Lymphoma (newly diagnosed, or if chemotherapy is no longer working) - Oral Melanoma or othertumor types (e.g., dogs with tumors of the skin, toes, mouth, perineum and other sites MAY be eligible). - Most internal tumors will NOT be eligible. - Patients may not receive anyother treatments for their tumor prior to, or during enrollment in study. Immunolight Therapy will be given spanning 3-5 weeks for: - Lymphoma patients - 15 treatment sessions, with follow-up visits at 1 and 2weeks after finishing treatment. If your pet is benefiting from Immunolight Therapy, then additional recheck visits will be required once a month for 5 more visits. - Solid tumor patients - 15 treatment sessions, with follow-up visits at 3 & 6 weeks, and 3 & 6 months. Study Benefits Include: - Variety of free initial staging tests - Free Immunolight Therapy sessions - Free follow-up visits - Compensation available (up to $250) This study is financially supported by Immunolight, LLC., and NC State CVM. More information about Immunolight Therapy, and study eligibility can be found at www.immunolight.com.

rows.title: Clinical trial for dogs with mast cell tumor.
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKIs), including toceranib (Palladia), are a class of drugs that are being used with increased frequency in both human and veterinary oncology. In both populations side effects occur in a large percentage of patients, with many requiring dose reductions or drug holidays, potentially impacting treatment success. Toceranib is used frequently in veterinary medicine and has been demonstrated to have a clinical benefit for dogs with a variety of tumor types including mast cell tumors, anal gland anal sac adenocarcinoma, thyroid carcinomas, head and neck carcinomas, nasal tumors, and metastatic osteosarcoma among others. The most commonly encountered side effects in dogs receiving toceranib are reported to be gastrointestinal (GI) in nature and include diarrhea, vomiting, reduced appetite and weight loss. The frequency and severity of these side effects is variable among individual dogs and currently there are no clinical or molecular makers to identify those dogs that would benefit from the use of medications to prevent GI side effects. This is critical as the development of GI side effects significantly impacts patient treatment. Importantly, dogs that develop GI side effects are less likely to remain on toceranib therapy due to a negative impact on quality of life. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this pilot study is to determine if plasma CK18 levels can be used as a biomarker that can predict GI side effects in dogs receiving toceranib.

rows.title: Use of CT/PET for soft tissue sarcoma histopathology grading

rows.description: The aim of the project is to determine the biologic behavior of sarcomas on PET/CT and correlate it with a more traditional histological grading system. rows.title: Effect of tumor-reducing prednisone on the staging of mast cell tumors in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To determine if administering prednisone prior to surgery affects the factors used to define the grade of mast cell tumors, and thus potentially affects prognosis and treatment recommendations. Background Mast cell tumors are the most common malignant skin tumor in dogs. The prognosis is highly-dependent upon the tumor grade, which can only be determined by histopathology (biopsy). For low-grade tumors, complete surgical removal is curative. However, nearly 100% of dogs with high-grade tumors will succumb to their disease within 6 months to a year of diagnosis. Treatment with prednisone is an effective treatment as sole therapy. It is also used prior to surgery to shrink the tumor or as part of a chemotherapy protocol used in dogs with high-grade tumors. However, it is unknown how the use of prednisone prior to surgery affects the factors used to define the tumor grade, which has potential to impact the prognosis and recommended further treatment options. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED

rows.title: Palladia®  and carboplatin combination chemotherapy in dogs with naturally-occurring cancer
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: Conventional chemotherapy protocols typically include one or sometimes multiple chemotherapeutic agents, that are directly toxic to the cancer cells, administered at maximally tolerated doses and intervals. Newer metronomic (low-dose continuous) chemotherapy protocols exert their anti-cancer activity differently, impacting the tumor microenvironment, angiogenesis and immune system. Furthermore, the mechanisms of acquired resistance to chemotherapy seem different when comparing high-dose conventional chemotherapeutic agents and metronomic agents. This is all strong evidence to support a combined treatment regimen.Toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) was the first veterinary anti-cancer agent to obtain FDA approval based on demonstrable safety and efficacy in the treatment of canine mast cell tumors. Toceranib has subsequently demonstrated benefit in the treatment of numerous canine malignancies. Toceranib has direct anti-cancer, as well as anti-angiogenic activity, and recent research suggests a role in immune system modulation. Previous studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison have clearly demonstrated that toceranib can be safely administered in combination with piroxicam, resulting in antitumor responses in canine carcinomas and sarcomas, in combination with CCNU, and doxorubicin, and vinblastine resulting in additive and synergistic effects in canine mast cell disease. Objective: The primary purpose of this study is to establish the safety and maximum tolerated dose of carboplatin when administered in combination with toceranib ( Palladia ) in dogs with malignant tumors. The secondary objective of this study is to demonstrate the efficacy/clinical benefit of this chemotherapeutic combination protocol in treating dogs with malignant tumors. What does enrollment into this trial involve? All dogs enrolled in this study will receive toceranib administered by mouth every other day for the duration of the study, and carboplatin administered intravenously every 21 days for a total of four treatments. Blood and urine samples will be collected at baseline, immediately prior to each subsequent dose of carboplatin, and 7, 14, and 21 days post-each dose of carboplatin. Imaging studies will be required for those patients with internal tumors only measurable with x-ray or ultrasound at least twice, but up to four times, during the study.After study day 84 (or sooner if your dog is removed from this study for any reason), the study will be completed and the oncology clinician will discuss additional and / or ongoing treatment options with you as the dogs owner and primary care giver. Client Compensation: The cost of the toceranib phosphate ( Palladia ) and carboplatin will be paid for by the study. Also covered will be the required recheck appointments, monitoring blood tests, urine tests, blood pressure evaluations and any imaging studies deemed necessary by the clinician. Treatment required for unanticipated side-effects will also be covered by the study up to $100. The owner is responsible for the costs of the initial appointment and the diagnostic work-up required prior to approval and enrollment in the study to ensure your dog is an appropriate study candidate, including the blood tests, urinalysis, blood pressure measurement and any imaging studies.

rows.title: Safety and efficacy of antibody therapy for dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer that commonly occurs in the spleen, liver, and the right side of the heart. The current standard of care for splenic hemangiosarcoma is surgical removal of the spleen followed by chemotherapy. Despite surgery and chemotherapy, the disease usually spreads and most dogs succumb to their disease within 6-12 months of diagnosis. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is a growth factor that may contribute to the spread and growth of hemangiosarcoma. In this clinical trial, we will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of an antibody therapy designed to inhibit VEGF and delay or prevent spread of the disease after surgery.

rows.title: Use of anti-CD47 antibodies as a treatment for equid skin tumors.
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: The usual treatment of solid equine skin tumors is complete surgical removal. If complete surgical removal is not possible, the usual treatment is surgical debulking and treatment of any remaining tumor with cryotherapy, laser therapy, chemotherapy, or radiation therapy. The purpose of this study is to investigate the treatment effects of an anti-CD47 antibody treatment on the destruction of tumor cells. Equine skin tumor cells have been shown to overexpress the CD47 protein, which may be key in preventing the destruction of the tumor cells. Blocking the protective effect of CD47 using the anti-CD47 antibody will ideally encourage phagocytosis of the tumor by macrophages. We have shown thus far that the antibody treatment is safe. No serious adverse effects have occurred in the cases enrolled and treated - one case developed a transient anemia. Some cases have been treated with control treatments; enrolling more cases will give us better information - as we can include greater numbers of treated cases. We have also seen that some of the treated cases had at least a transient decrease in tumor size.

rows.title: Reversal of Myeloid Cell Immune Suppression with a CCR2 Inhibitor Combined with a Myeloid Cell Depleting Agent for Treatment of Os
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that a certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib (PalladiaTM) is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins important for cancer growth called receptor tyrosine kinases. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib as well. In addition, we have discovered that the angiotensin receptor blocking (ARB) drug losartan also functions to block monocyte activity. In recent studies, we have also determined that treatment with the combination of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as toceranib, together with losartan exerts significantly greater antitumor activity than either drug alone.

rows.title: Canine lymphoma treated with prednisone (steroid) only
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Background: Currently, there is no well-defined study regarding the survival and quality of life for dogs with lymphoma treated with prednisone, an orally administered, inexpensive steroid, despite the drug's inclusion in almost every treatment protocol for lymphoma. Why prednisone? Chemotherapy for canine lymphoma is costly, time-consuming, and has a risk of serious complications. Prednisone is thought to improve quality of life and reduce lymph node size. But the benefit of this inexpensive, orally administered drug has not been formally studied. Purpose of Study: The Canine LYmPhoma Steriod Only (CALYPSO) is a multi-center study involving 100 dogs with high grade lymphoma from approximately 15 contributing veterinary schools and specialty practices.We are interested in determining the response to therapy, how long does it last, if certain types of lymphoma respond better than others to prednisone, and most importantly, how quality of life is improved. Does my dog qualify for the study? Participant dogs need a confirmed diagnosis of intermediate to high-grade lymphoma. Your veterinarian can send aspirates or tissue samples for analysis to the laboratory of her/his choice or we can do this for you at the hospital. Dogs with lymphoma in peripheral lymph nodes qualify for the study. Dogs with skin or gastrointestinal lymphoma are not eligible for the study.Dogs with lymphoma in the spleen and liver only without peripheral lymph node involvement are not eligible.Dogs receiving any chemotherapy or prednisone before they visit our hospital are not eligible. What happens during the study? On the first day, your dogs quality of life at home will be assessed by having you answer questions about how he/she is feeling. This questionnaire will be repeated on Day 7, Day 14, and then monthly thereafter.Someone will contact you at home and review the questions with you if you do not revisit the hospital. Because the response to prednisone may differ between dogs based on the type of lymphoma (T-cell or B-cell), a fine needle aspiration of a lymph node will be obtained at the beginning of the study so it can be sent to a lab for special staining. After routine lab tests and a thorough physical exam including lymph node measurements are completed, your dog will start taking prednisone daily by mouth at home.All dogs get the same dosage.

rows.title: Phenotypic characterization of peripheral blood monocytes in canine osteosarcoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer in dogs. Even after surgical tumor removal and chemotherapy, the cancer often spreads (metastasizes) and dogs usually die of metastatic disease within an average of 12 months after diagnosis, despite aggressive therapy. However, interestingly, survival times have been shown to sometimes double in osteosarcoma patients who develop infections associated with surgical removal of the primary tumor. These infections may be capable of activating white blood cells such as monocytes to promote anti-tumor activity. The role of monocytes needs to be better understood in general in order to exploit their anti-tumor capabilities. Study Objective The purpose of this study is to characterize differences of monocytes between normal dogs, and osteosarcoma dogs. This will help us define changes that occur in monocytes of an osteosarcoma dog and enhance our understanding of the monocytes ability for tumor suppression. Our long-term goal is to harness the anti-tumor potential of monocytes to develop new therapies using these cells to increase survival in osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? We are recruiting dogs in five different categories: 1.Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent limb amputation and full course of standard chemotherapy (no clinical trial dogs), one or more months after final chemo, no maximum amount of time. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. 2. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and have underwent a limb-sparing surgery and have been diagnosed with a limb-spare associated infection. Samples that qualify for this category can be collected off-site and shipped to NCSU. This study will cover the cost of overnight shipping. 3. Dogs that have been diagnosed with osteosarcoma and not yet undergone treatment. These dogs can be enrolled at any time after diagnosis, just prior to treatment to include amputation. These dogs must be free of pulmonary metastasis. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign an informed consent for venipuncture. Blood will be drawn from each patient, either at time of diagnosis prior to commencement of any therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation) orafter definitive treatment (amputation/stereotactic radiation + chemotherapy) has been completed. rows.title: Cancer pain in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Background - Recognition and alleviation of pain in oncology patients is essential for maintaining quality of life. Pain in these patients may be due to the cancer itself, a treatment modality being used (e.g., radiation or surgery), or a concurrent disease (e.g., osteoarthritis). To adequately control pain, a combination of more than one pain medication (NSAIDs, opioids, and adjuvant drugs such as gabapentin) is routinely required. Practitioners have at their disposal comprehensive sources of information on pain management. Most notably, the recently updated AAHA/AAFP Pain Management Guidelines for Dogs and Cats provide current recommendations for a multimodal approach to preempting and controlling pain. However, too much is often as deleterious (if not more) than not enough, in pain management! Aim - To put in adequacy pain management with pain mechanisms in cancerous canine patients, while establishing a pain mechanisms-based approach for analgesia in canine oncology. Design - Prospective, longitudinally open, baseline-controlled clinical trial. Methodology - Client-owned dogs affected by cancer (exclusion: lymphoma, mastocytoma, visceral hemangiosarcoma, and multiple myeloma) will be refereed to CVRS Oncology service for entering in an original study establishing pain mechanisms in cancerous dogs requiring palliative care. In addition to physical examination, clinical pathology tests, and global (visual analogue scale - VAS) pain assessment by the oncologist, global assessment by the owner (VAS, and canine health-related quality of life index - CHQLI), cinematic assessment (static stance weight-bearing and accelerometry), quantitative sensory tests (QST) will characterize the pain profile of the cancerous dog: * Primary punctate mechanical threshold, primary dynamic tactile threshold, secondary mechanical threshold, and conditioned pain modulation would respectively establish the presence of peripheral and/or central sensitization, as well as the value of diffuse nociceptive inhibitory control. * Analgesia would follow a step-wise approach, including NSAID (cimicoxib), anticonvulsant (gabapentin), and tricyclic antidepressant (amitriptyline). Cimicoxib is expected to target inflammatory peripheral / central sensitization. Gabapentin, as calcium channel blocker, would counteract spinal windup. Amitriptyline, as serotonine / noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, would re-enforce descending inhibitory controls. The whole duration of follow-up would be less than one month, including 5 consultations for assuring animal welfare assessment, detection of potential drug side effects. and potential requirement to rescue analgesia. Potential benefits - To improve the quality of care provided to patients affected with cancer.

rows.title: Brain Tumor Tissue Biobanking
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study to bank tissues from canine brain tumors, for shared use by investigators nationally, to better understand tumor behavior and develop new treatments. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of your pets brain tumor as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). In this case the clinical trial is to collect brain tumor and other tissues that will be used in numerous other future studies evaluating these topics. Your pets clinician and the Clinical Trials team will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Lack of access to good quality canine brain tumor tissues and tumor cell cultures is the biggest barrier in advancing the field of brain tumor investigation and therapeutic development. Very few veterinary institutions in this country have an actively-funded tumor biorepository, and fewer actively acquire and bank brain tumor tissues. Where canine biobanks exist, brain tumors remain strikingly underrepresented. Thus, there is a great importance to collecting and banking canine brain tumor tissues for shared use among comparative brain cancer researchers. Comprehensive information about tumor genetics, biology, and the molecular landscape of brain tumors, will allow specific determination of which pathways or tumor types/subtypes provide the best model for comparative and translational studies to advance human therapies. The availability of comprehensive data from the canine model will help promote identification and development of novel therapeutics that are targeted to molecular pathways or triggers for cancer development that co-occur in humans and dogs, and identify appropriate use of canine clinical trials that may promote more rapid approval of novel therapeutics through regulatory mechanisms. Tissues from the CSU Tissue Repository are made available to other institutions that wish to collaborate brain tumor studies, so the collection and banking of brain tumor tissues here at CSU will have far-reaching benefits to other institutions as well. The NIH National Cancer Institutes Comparative Brain Tumor Consortium (of which CSU is a member and active participant) already has in place collaborations among several key players in the area of brain tumor research, many of whom are in need of brain tumor specimens for their studies in tumor genetics, molecular biology, and therapeutic development. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? Dogs must have a diagnosis of a brain tumor that is deemed surgically resectable/accessible based on MRI characteristics. They cannot have had any prior radiation therapy or chemotherapy for their tumor. They must have good function of the liver and kidneys, have acceptable blood counts, and be free of severe underlying disease that might affect safe administration of anesthesia. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing prior to starting the study to ensure that they are eligible, including blood work (complete blood count, chemistry profile), urinalysis, and brain MRI. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? After eligibility is confirmed, your dog will go under anesthesia for brain tumor resection. During surgery, the tumor tissue will be removed and evaluated by histopathology to obtain a diagnosis, as normally occurs with any clinical case. A portion of the tumor tissues collected will be processed and stored in the tissue biobank, for future use in various investigations of brain tumor biology or development of novel treatments. In addition to tumor tissue, blood, a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid, and a small sample of skin from the edge of the incision, will also be collected and banked. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? The act of tissue banking has no inherent risk, and this tumor tissue would normally be removed surgically; however, your pet may experience side effects associated with brain tumor surgery. The surgical technique has been used in veterinary brain tumor resection routinely. Nevertheless, surgery of any kind, and in particular surgery within the brain, does have risks associated with it, which could be mild or severe (including death). Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician or Clinical Trials team. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? After surgery is complete, your pets participation in the clinical trial is finished. Your pets clinician will discuss options for continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician and/or the Clinical Trials team if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets brain tumor. The clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? The study will apply a credit of up to $8000 to your VTH account to be put towards the costs of brain surgery. These credits can only be applied after your dog has been deemed eligible and you have chosen to enter the trial, and will be credited to your account after surgery is completed. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for any and all other costs relating to your dogs care not covered by the study, including the cost of the initial examination and pre-anesthesia testing required prior to entering the study or after the study ends, any costs of diagnostic testing or treatment beyond those covered by the credit, as well as any optional adjunctive cancer therapies you might elect. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets clinician or the Clinical Trials team if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. rows.title: CT for detection of metastasis in canine oral malignant melanoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Currently, there is no standardized approach in veterinary medicine to assess for metastasis in oral malignant melanoma in dogs. Previous research has found that feelinglymph nodes on examination can be an inaccurate assessment for cancer spread as they can be normal in size and still contain tumor cells. Needle aspirates of lymph nodes can be obtained to evaluate for evidence of spread at the cellular level, but there are several lymph nodes in the head and neck region which can be involved, and some are difficult to access on examination. Some of these lymph nodes are not generally found on physical examination, require advanced imaging to be detected, and can be challenging to acquire aspirates. Advanced imaging most commonly includes a neck ultrasound or a computed tomography (CT) scan of the region. This is part of the reason for the CT scan in your dog. This scan allows for better determination of the extent of the primary tumor, but also the lymph node appearance. As such, CTs are commonly used for surgical and/or radiation planning.As a diagnostic regularly utilized in current practice, we seek to determine whether CT is a sensitive and specific indicator for lymph node metastasis in dogs with oral malignant melanoma. In human medicine, staging for similar head and neck tumors also regularly includes the functional imaging positron emission tomography (PET) combined with CT, which assesses for regions of increased metabolic activity and has been found to correspond with cancer in the body. Currently, the accuracy for prediction of metastasis as well as for the local extent of disease is unknown for PET/CT in canine melanoma. In this study, palpation, CT, and PET appearance of lymph nodes of your dog will be compared to histopathologic (biopsy)results. We hypothesize that CT and PET will provide an increased sensitivity and specificity over palpation alone and will be accurate enough to eliminate unnecessary sampling or resection of lymph nodes in the future.

rows.title: Melanocortin 4 Receptor Antagonist in the Treatment of Canine Cachexia
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Cachexia is defined as weight loss and muscle atrophy that cannot be reversed by consuming more calories. This can occur in humans and animals with chronic illnesses, such as cancer, heart disease, and kidney disease. It has also been associated with a worse prognosis in these diseases. The melanocortin pathway in the central nervous system is believed to be a major player in the control of food intake and metabolism. Activation of melanocortin receptors in the brain leads to decreased food intake and increased metabolism. By blocking these receptors with a novel drug, the hope is that pets will have increased food intake and decreased metabolism, resulting in weight gain. Preclinical studies suggest that this new MC4R antagonist will improve appetite, energy level, and weight gain, providing an overall improvement in quality of life. The goal of this study is to determine the side effects and effectiveness of a new melanocortin 4 receptor antagonist in the treatment of canine cachexia.

rows.title: LNMRI for Diagnosing Metastatic Lymph Nodes

Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. A secondary goal of this trial is to evaluate any anti-tumor effects it may have in dogs with sarcomas. If the exams, tests, and procedures show that your dog can take part in the study, and you choose to enroll them, then the following will happen as part of the study: On the first day your dog receives the new drug, they will have blood drawn at multiple time points and will be in hospital for close monitoring for at least 8 hours after their first dose. They will receive a tablet daily and be rechecked 1, 2, 4, and 6 weeks after starting then every 4 weeks thereafter, as long as their disease is not worsening, and the drug is well tolerated. On these follow-up visits, we will collect additional blood, both to assess how they are handling the drug and to store for research purposes.
