rows.title: Treating soft tissue sarcomas in dogs with non-surgical ultrasound ablation
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose To evaluate the activity of a type of communication signal released from cells in dogs with soft tissue sarcomas after they are treated with non-invasive histotripsy ablation Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of skin cancer in dogs. They tend to develop slowly and dont usually metastasize when they are low grade. A biopsy is needed to determine the tumor grade. Surgery is the treatment of choice, but if a minimal surgery (removal of only the tumor that can be seen or felt) is performed, the tumor is likely to grow back. Removal of the tumor and several centimeters of normal-appearing tissue is required for complete removal. However, this can be impossible without amputation or the addition of radiation therapy, particularly when the tumors are large or affect certain areas of the body like the limbs or face. Alternative treatments to surgery or radiation are needed. We have previously evaluated a non-surgical, non-radiation, non-thermal focused ultrasound treatment (histotripsy) to kill soft tissue sarcomas affecting pet dogs. This technology has also been used in humans with liver tumors. Histotripsy focuses microsecond-long soundwaves through the skin onto a precise target area of the tumor. This causes air bubbles in the tumor tissue to expand and collapse, mechanically disintegrating the surrounding tumor tissue. Research in rodents, pet dogs, and humans have shown that the liquified tissue stimulates the immune system to recognize cancer in other parts of the body. The purpose of this study is to evaluate one type of communication signal released from cells, termed extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs carry protein and genetic messages that cause immediate changes in the receiving cell. EVs and their cargo can be used as a non-invasive way to diagnose a tumor or look for signals to predict response to treatment or prognosis. We will extract and measure EVs and their immune signal cargo from the liquified tumor tissue, the lymph nodes, and the blood after histotripsy treatment of soft tissue sarcomas. We hope to find that histotripsy increases the number and type of EVs in the blood, which would be the first step in developing a liquid biopsy for diagnosis; we also hope to find that histotripsy treatment changes the communication with the immune system, serving as a mechanism to explain the changes seen in the immune response after histotripsy. To determine how histotripsy may affect EVs, we are recruiting dogs with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo histotripsy treatment of the tumor. An existing tumor must be present for treatment. The application of this experimental therapy has the potential to directly enhance the quality of life of dogs diagnosed with soft tissue sarcomas and defray the cost of treatment. At the same time, the results of our study may lead to improved liquid biopsy and treatment options for human cancer patients.

In the field of veterinary oncology, identification of metastatic disease is critical for determining
the extent of disease, prognosis, and for developing treatment plans. For many cancer types,
metastasis occurs via the lymphatic system and the status of the draining lymph nodes is an
important part of the pre- and intraoperative evaluation. The sentinel lymph node (SLN) is the
primary lymph node draining the tumour and although one might expect that it is the first lymph
node downstream from the tumour, this is not always true. Failure to identify and assess the
sentinel lymph node can lead to incomplete treatment, worse prognosis and poor patient outcome.
Currently in veterinary patients, there are not good protocols in place to identify sentinel lymph
nodes. The development of these protocols could help us to decrease the number of lymph nodes
we remove, in addition to ensuring we are accurately evaluating the most important lymph node
for making follow-up treatment recommendations.

You will be responsible for bringing your pet to the OVC-HSC for both the CT scan and surgery
(may occur during the same visit). In addition, you are expected to pay for the standard costs for
the preoperative staging, including the CT scan and surgery for removal of the tumour and lymph
nodes. Like any medication, the clinical trial treatment may have a low rate of side effects. This
study does not cover the costs of hospitalization or other costs associated with complications
related or unrelated to the clinical trial.
You are expected to return to the Ontario Veterinary College for follow-up appointments as
outlined by your clinician and the clinical trial protocol.

The commitment to participate in this study is no different than if your pet was undergoing a CT
scan and surgery for their tumour. In this study, we are considering what is already standard of
care (CT and surgery) and trying to improve this process. For the CT scan, in addition to
receiving a contrast agent intravenously, as is always performed for these cases, we will also
inject a similar agent locally. With this injection, we will attempt to identify the lymph node that
first drains the tumour, also known as the sentinel lymph node. This information will be
compared to our findings in surgery and on histopathology when the tissues are submitted.
Following the procedure, your pet will be monitored for several hours to ensure they do not
develop any complications from the injection. Surgery will be planned for within 1 week of the
CT scan and may be as soon as the day following.

return for surgery following routine planning. To be included in the study, your pet must have
surgery within 1 week of the CT scan to ensure that no major changes in the tumour growth have

Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

rows.title: Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.


Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated. In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity). After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication. This is an out-patient procedure.

rows.title: A dose-finding study of Paccal Vet in cats with spontaneous solid tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
No chemotherapies have been FDA-approved for use in cats despite a growing need for such therapies. Paclitaxel (Taxol®) is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer therapy today, with potent activity against a variety of cancers in people that also occur in cats. Paclitaxel has been found to kill cancer cell lines isolated from cat tumors in the laboratory, but only one small study has been published evaluating paclitaxel treatment of cats with cancer. In that study, 5 of 9 patients responded to paclitaxel therapy, with 4 of these patients experiencing stable disease and one patient experiencing a partial response. 


The current FDA-approved formulation of paclitaxel for use in people, which uses a cremophor-based agent to solubilize the drug for injection, causes allergic reactions in dogs and cats. This characteristic of the FDA-approved formulation has largely prevented its use in pets. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal® Vet, uses a formulation that has been created to minimize allergic reactions and therefore improve tolerability. Several clinical trials have been performed or are ongoing with this formulation in dogs, but to date, no studies in cats using Paccal Vet have been undertaken. 


The primary purpose of this study is to test the tolerability of Paccal Vet in cats and to determine an acceptable dose. A secondary, exploratory goal is to see whether Paccal Vet may have anti-tumor activity in various tumors in cats. In this context, “exploratory” means that this study is not large enough to prove whether or not Paccal Vet is working in feline cancer. However, the results could help the drug developer determine whether the drug might have the potential to do so. 


The “investigational” part of the study is to test whether Paccal Vet is safe for use in cats and whether the drug may induce an anti-tumor response against their cancer. Paccal Vet is an investigational drug, which means it has not yet been approved by the FDA for use in dogs or cats. The potential benefits and safety of Paccal Vet in the treatment of cats with various cancer types have not yet been demonstrated. The purpose of this study is to test the investigational use of Paccal Vet rather than to provide medical treatment to your cat.


Cats enrolled in the study will receive Paccal Vet via intravenous infusion over 15-30 minutes once every 3 weeks for up to four doses. Throughout those treatment cycles, cats will be monitored carefully for tumor responses and adverse events through physical examinations, blood work, and quality of life questionnaires.

rows.title: Treating Dogs With Glioma Using Radiation and Immunotherapy
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Gliomas are aggressive primary brain tumors that pose significant therapeutic challenges in both human and veterinary medicine. In dogs, gliomas are characterized by locally invasive growth and poor overall survival, even with intervention. Brachycephalic breeds—particularly French Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, and Boxers—are disproportionately affected, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition that remains under investigation.

Current treatment strategies for canine glioma typically involve surgical resection when anatomically feasible, followed by adjuvant radiation therapy. Radiotherapy may also be used as a standalone treatment, delivered through various approaches, including conventionally fractionated protocols or stereotactic radiation therapy (SRT). SRT offers the advantages of high precision, greater tissue sparing, and shorter treatment duration. Despite these interventions, the prognosis remains guarded, with median survival times often not exceeding 12 months.

Canine gliomas share many biological, imaging, and histopathological features with human glioblastoma (GBM), the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. As such, dogs with spontaneous glioma represent a highly relevant veterinary patient population for translational research aimed at improving outcomes in human neuro-oncology. Their natural disease course, intact immune system, and clinically comparable treatment environment make canine models especially valuable for evaluating the efficacy and safety of emerging therapies.

One promising frontier in glioma treatment is immunotherapy. In this study, we investigate the combination of stereotactic radiation therapy with an FDA-approved nanoparticle, previously shown to be safe in dogs. This nanoparticle has demonstrated the ability in rodent models to modulate the tumor immune microenvironment by transforming tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) from an M2 (pro-tumor) to an M1 (anti-tumor) phenotype.

Building upon these encouraging results, our current research proposes to evaluate the combined therapeutic effect of CAR immunotherapy and radiation therapy in dogs diagnosed with glioma. The rationale is to transform the tumor microenvironment through CAR neutrophils, potentially enhancing the efficacy and outcome of radiation therapy. This synergistic approach may not only improve survival in canine patients but also provide critical translational insights for the treatment of glioblastoma in humans.

Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.

rows.title: Non-invasive treatment of oral tumors in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Purpose

To evaluate the effects of histotripsy, a high-precision ultrasound-based treatment that can non-invasively destroy tumor tissue without radiation or heat, on dogs with oral tumors. 


Background

Histotripsy is an emerging technology that uses focused ultrasound waves to mechanically destroy tumor tissue. Histotripsy has the ability to precisely destroy tumors non-invasively and without using heat or radiation. Histotripsy also has the potential to stimulate the immune system into fighting off remaining or microscopic tumor. Our team’s previous research has evaluated the safety and efficacy of histotripsy for bone tumors, soft tissue sarcomas, and brain tumors in dogs. Additionally, histotripsy was FDA-approved for the treatment of liver tumors in humans in 2023, with promising clinical results. We are now interested in how histotripsy affects oral tumors in dogs. 


Study Design

Dogs will undergo CT and/or MRI scans (if not obtained previously during diagnostics) to visualize the oral tumor and plan the histotripsy treatment. The histotripsy treatment approach will be patient-specific to accommodate for unique tumor sizes and locations.  

On the day of treatment, hair will be removed from the area overlying the tumor to allow for maximum transmission of the ultrasound waves. Histotripsy treatment will be delivered non-invasively through the skin to mechanically disintegrate the underlying tumor. Dogs will be maintained and monitored under anesthesia. After the treatment, images (CT and/or MRI) will be taken to assess the immediate effects of the ultrasound treatment. Most patients recover uneventfully and go home the same day.

One day after the completion of histotripsy treatment, dogs will undergo standard-of-care surgical resection. This allows us to assess the effects of the ultrasound treatment. At this point, participation in the study is complete.

rows.title: Histotripsy ultrasound therapy effectiveness on equine sarcoids
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Background

Equine sarcoids are the most common skin tumors in horses, associated with bovine papillomavirus (BPV). These locally invasive tumors lead to lesions that cause discomfort, pain, and functional limitations, significantly impacting a horse’s quality of life. Sarcoids are persistent and prone to recurrence, making their removal essential for preventing complications like infections or interference with tack. Current treatments, including surgery and cryotherapy, can be invasive, inconsistent, and have high recurrence rates, emphasizing the need for novel, effective solutions.

Histotripsy is a non-invasive ultrasound therapy that uses focused ultrasound waves to create microbubbles that mechanically disrupt targeted tissue. Unlike thermal methods, histotripsy’s non-thermal mechanism ensures precise ablation with minimal damage to surrounding tissues. Developed for human medicine, histotripsy shows promise in veterinary applications due to its precision, real-time imaging, and adaptability.

Non-invasive therapeutics like histotripsy are vital for improving animal welfare, minimizing recovery time, and reducing risks associated with invasive procedures. For equine sarcoids, histotripsy could offer a safe, precise, and effective alternative that could transform treatment outcomes and set a new standard of care for equine cutaneous neoplasia.

rows.title: 3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat.


3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach.


Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. Some of these follow-up visits can be done with your regular veterinarian if you choose; however, the study will not be able to cover the costs of these visits.

rows.title: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.

rows.title: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.

rows.title: Phase I study of KPT-9274 in dogs with lymphoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study: PAK4 is a protein present in cells that is involved in helping to control the rate of cell growth. In normal cells, PAK 4 is tightly regulated so that growth occurs in a normal ordered manner. It is now known that abnormalities occur in PAK4 in cancer cells that contribute to driving uncontrolled tumor growth. In some cells there are mutations in PAK4 that cause it to be turned on all the time, and in others its expression is very high causing the tumor cells to divide uncontrollably. Based on the role of PAK4 in cancer there has been great interest in developing inhibitors of this protein that can be used to treat tumors and possibly halt their growth. Karyopharm Therapeutics has developed a drug called KPT-9274 that is given orally and binds to PAK4, thereby blocking its ability to drive cell growth. KPT-9274 has shown good activity against tumor cell lines in the laboratory and also inhibits tumor growth in mouse models of cancer. KPT-9274 has been tested in normal dogs and is well tolerated with no side effects when given at doses between1.5-6 mg/kg orally given on a Monday/Thursday or Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule. KPT-9274 has also been tested in dogs with cancer, and doses ranging from 2-4 mg per given on a Monday/Wednesday/Friday schedule for 28 days were not associated with any side effects. Objective of the trial: The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the activity of KPT-9274 when given in combination with doxorubicin chemotherapy for the treatment of canine lymphoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - A diagnosis of lymphoma (T or B cell, newly diagnosed). - Dogs must be free of other diseases (heart, liver, and kidney) and be feeling good (playing, good appetite). - Your dog will be screened for eligibility based on bloodwork (complete blood count, biochemistry profile, urinalysis, chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound) What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? If enrolled dogs will receive KPT-9274 for 4 doses (Monday/Wednesday/Friday/Monday followed by the administration of doxorubicin 24 hours after the last dose of KPT-9274. Recheck exams will be performed weekly (days 14, 21, and 28) for 1 month, then monthly thereafter. Routine bloodwork and urinalysis will be performed at these visits. Client Compensation All costs for the first 4 weeks of the clinical trial are covered, and a credit of $500 will be available for standard of care chemotherapy if/when your dog should fail treatment with the drug combination. If your dog does well (i.e., achieves a complete remission for over 28 days) with the treatment combination, then you will be offered an opportunity to re-treat with the drug combination. For retreatment, KPT-9274 will be offered at no cost, although you will be responsible for the administration of the doxorubicin.

rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Feline gastrointestinal (GI) lymphoblastic lymphoma (FGLL) is a debilitating disease of older cats. Chemotherapy for treatment of FGLL has been used with limited success and long-term survival is uncommon. Radiation therapy (RT) is used to treat localized lymphoma in humans and in two small studies of cats with lymphoma confined to the intestinal tract treated with RT, clinical signs improved in most cats. The purpose of this study is to determine whether the addition of abdominal cavity RT to oral chemotherapy (lomustine), daily oral prednisone, and weekly parenteral cobalamin will improve response to therapy, survival times, and quality of life of affected cats. If the addition of RT improves outcome, this therapy may be adopted as the standard of care for cats with FGLL and may be used to further study the use of RT for lymphocytic lymphoma and inflammatory bowel disease. Eligibility: - Cats with a cytologic or histologic diagnosis of FGLL (to include stomach, small intestine, large intestine, pancreas, mesenteric lymph nodes, and/or liver) - An expected survival of > 3 weeks regardless of therapy - Baseline ALT and total bilirubin < 2 x baseline Exclusion Criteria: - Cats with obstructing intestinal masses that are amenable to surgery - Patients that have received prednisone or other chemotherapy drugs < 14 days prior to enrollment in the study

rows.title: Evaluation of biomarkers as risk factors for lymphoma in Golden Retrievers.
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: The purpose of this study is to identify aberrant epigenetic (DNA methylation) changes in lymphoma cells to develop biomarkers of each class of lymphoma, and in turn, identify new therapy targets for affected Golden Retrievers. More significantly, because DNA methylation changes occur so early in the process of cancer formation, these investigators hypothesize that they could serve as biomarkers of risk, allowing medicine or diet to prevent lymphoma in Golden Retrievers before it develops. Finally, they propose to fully phenotype cancer stem cells in lymphoma by surface markers and DNA methylation changes for the purpose of targeting those cells which feed cancer metastasis. Individually each project advances a current frontier of research. By performing them in parallel, the discoveries made in each project can be combined, correlated, and translated into biomarkers of risk, diagnosis, and prognosis to advance the prevention and management of lymphoma in Golden Retrievers. The goal is the establishment of genetic risk alleles, defining the gene expression profile and the role of cellular activation in lymphoma and hemangiosarcoma. Title: Evaluation of biomarkers as risk factors for lymphoma in Golden Retrievers. rows.title: Photodynamic Therapy for Canine Lung Tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose of the Study: Photodynamic therapy combines a drug, known as a photosensitizing agent, with a specific type of light, commonly laser, to kill cells. The goal of this study is to determine if photodynamic therapy would be useful in treating dog and potentially human lung tumors. The steps of photodynamic therapy include injection of a photosensitizing agent into the blood. The drug is absorbed all over the body, but stays in cancer cells slightly longer than in normal cells. Two days after drug absorption, the tumor is exposed to a light source. Photosensitizer agents in the cells absorb the light and produce an active form of oxygen which destroys nearby cells. Patient Entry Criteria: Eligible patients include dogs having a single lung tumor greater than 2 centimeters in diameter. The patient will need to have a needle aspirate taken of the tumor which confirms a diagnosis of carcinoma prior to enrollment. Also recent chest radiographs, a complete blood count, a serum biochemistry panel, and a urinalysis are necessary prior to enrollment. The study is limited to dogs not having evidence of metastatic disease and who are in otherwise good health. What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? Each dog will receive an intravenous injection of a photosensitizing agent on Day 0. Two days later on Day 2, each dog will be anesthetized for a chest CT scan and additional outpatient procedures. Following the CT scan while still anesthetized, a bronchoscopy (a flexible camera placed inside the trachea and lung airway branches) will be combined with fluoroscopy (a version of real-time chest xray imaging) to deliver a lighted wire through the bronchoscope for temporary placement into the lung tumor of each dog. Just prior to the lighted wire placement, a second photosensitizing agent acid will be given either orally or intravenously. Once the lighted wire has been activated to stimulate photosensitizing drugs within the lung tumor to cause cell death, the wire and scope will be removed. Two days later on Day 4, each dog will be readmitted to the hospital for routine surgical removal of the lung tumor via traditional thoracic surgery. Reevaluation with the Clinical Trials team at Colorado State University will be expected at two weeks, four weeks, and six weeks after the traditional thoracic surgery. Your pet will experience side effects. Specifically, dogs will experience light sensitivity, or photosensitivity, following administration of the photosensitizing drugs. The light sensitivity is expected to last from two to six weeks, the estimated amount of time for the drugs to be eliminated from the body. It is anticipated the ears may be the most sensitive to side effect, and will be a barometer for overall photosensitivity, but any exposed or lightly haired area of the body is susceptible including the belly, mouth, and eye tissues. Any strong light, including indoor as well as sunlight, could affect photosensitivity. Thus dogs will need to be kept mostly indoors during the time period of about one month, until the drugs are metabolized. Use of sunscreen products will not be of benefit. Dogs will need to be protected against unrestricted outdoor sunlight exposure in the first month following treatment by being supervised on a leash long enough to allow for urinations and defecations. If the ears become red or show signs suggestive of a 'sun burn' while a dog is being quarantined indoors, then less use of bright indoor lights will be recommended to reduce exposure effects. Importantly, controlled light exposure is the key for metabolism of the photosensitizing agents. Combined use of two photosensitizing agents in this study is anticipated to reduce the light sensitivity side effects in dogs. Owner Responsibilities: You are responsible for an initial examination, complete blood count, serum biochemistry profile, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs, and needle-aspiration diagnosis of your dogs tumor. You are also responsible for the costs associated with your dogs traditional thoracic surgery (minus the $1000 credit), for recheck fees at the fourth- and sixth-week visits following traditional thoracic surgery, and any other tests recommended by your pets oncologist. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Financial Incentives: Enrollment in this clinical trial provides a $1000 credit to be used towards your pets traditional thoracic surgery for removal of the lung tumor. Enrollment in the trial also includes a free CT scan, bronchoscopy, and fluoroscopy, studies valued at over $2000.

rows.title: Treatment of bone cancer in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: The Morris Animal Foundation and the National Cancer Institute are sponsoring a clinical trial in dogs with newly diagnosed Osteosarcoma. This trial is being conducted by the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium. 180 dogs will be enrolled in this study. All dogs will receive surgical removal of their tumor and receive standard of care chemotherapy. Dogs will be randomized at time of enrollment to either receive standard of care alone or standard of care with orally administered rapamycin. Eligibility: Confirmed osteosarcoma diagnosis. Has not received any prior treatment for osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common bone tumor in dogs. Amputation and chemotherapy significantly improves median survival times for dogs with this tumor type, from around 4-6 months to around 10-12 months. However, most dogs are not cured, and die due to the spread of their disease (metastasis) within 1-2 years. Better treatment options to treat cancer spread are needed to improve survival time for these patients. Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a drug that works through the blockade of mTOR, a cellular pathway that is associated with tumor spread. Preliminary studies have been performed in cell lines, in mice, and in dogs that demonstrate anti-tumor activity. Previous studies have also established a safe dose in healthy dogs and dogs with cancer. The addition of this drug to standard amputation followed by carboplatin chemotherapy is hoped to delay or prevent tumor spread, thus improving patient survival. All dogs receive the current recommended therapy for osteosarcoma (standard of care: SOC), consisting of amputation followed by 4 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy, given 3 weeks apart, initiated within 10-14 days of surgery. Your dog will then be randomly assigned to enter the study group that receives SOC alone, or the group that has the addition of the drug rapamycin (Rapa). All dogs in both groups will return every two months for monitoring for disease progression, including chest radiographs. Rapamycin is an oral drug, given at home, daily on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday of each week, with no drug administered on Fridays, Saturdays, or Sundays for a total of four months. Additional visits for the Rapa group of dogs includes 5 overnight stays (two the first month, then 3 additional monthly visits) for the purposes of a 24 hour blood collection to determine the levels of the drug in your dog's body. In order to minimize the number of times your dog's vein must be punctured for blood collection, a central venous catheter will be placed, under minor sedation.

rows.title: Evaluation of safety and effectiveness of adjuvant oral rapamycin following standard of care therapy in dogs with bone tumors (ost
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Explanation of Study This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and sponsored by the Morris Animal Foundation seeks to evaluate in dogs with osteosarcoma the safety and effectiveness of adjuvant oral rapamycin following Standard of Care therapy. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on an every 21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been shown to safely and effectively improve survival in dogs with appendicular osteosarcoma for over 20 years. ALL dogs enrolled onto study will receive Standard of Care (SOC) therapy; however, through a randomization process, some dogs entered into study will also receive additional therapy with oral rapamycin. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved to induce immunosuppression in human patients receiving organ and bone marrow transplants. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs (rapalogs) in human patients, suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Study Objective This study will evaluate if orally administered rapamycin following SOC therapy improves long-term disease control in dogs with osteosarcoma. What qualifies my dog for enrollment in this trial? To participate in this clinical trial your dog must have: - Confirmed diagnosis of osteosarcoma - Primary appendicular osteosarcoma that is amenable to surgical removal via amputation (No evidence that the tumor has spread to the lung (metastasis) based upon physical exam, thoracic radiographs, and abdominal ultrasound). - ONLY newly diagnosed dogs are eligible with no prior therapy (conventional or metronomic chemotherapy, ionizing radiation, bisphosphonates) for osteosarcoma. - Dogs receiving analgesics including NSAIDs, gabapentin, tramadol, or other will be eligible for study inclusion. What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? To enroll in this study, you must sign informed consent allowing the surgical amputation of your dog's affected limb. Following amputation, your dog will return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 3 weeks for 15 weeks for evaluation. On weeks 3, 6, 9 and 12 your dog will receive a dose of carboplatin. Precautions should be taken against contact with your dog's urine or feces for 48 hours after carboplatin treatment. Blood work will be done on your dog prior to carboplatin administration. After completion of SOC therapy, and depending upon initial study randomization, you might be required to administer oral rapamycin (PO) at home for 4 months. The schedule for rapamycin administration will be daily on Monday-Thursday (4 days on), with a drug holiday on Friday, Saturday and Sunday (no dosing, 3 days off). This will allow us to determine if oral rapamycin can be safely administered chronically and will require serial collections of blood on scheduled reevaluations to allow for measurements of rapamycin within your dog's blood. Your dog will have a total of five 24-hour serial blood draws completed over the course of 4 months. At the end of the each study cycle (Day 25), your dog must return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital for reassessment and further blood collections. If your dog has been randomized to receive oral rapamycin, these visits are required for inclusion in the study. If your dog is in the Standard of Care arm only, you will be required to return to the NCSU Veterinary Hospital every 8 weeks for evaluation. Client Compensation Following determination of your dog's eligibility and limb amputation, costs associated with this study will be provided, including a $1000 hospital credit towards your dog's limb amputation. Client Contact NCSU Clinical Studies Core: cvmclinicalstudies@ncsu.edu for more information about this study.

rows.title: Evaluating a targeted her2/neu cancer vaccine for the stimulation of anti-tumor immunity and prolonging survival times in dogs wit
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Transitional cell carcinoma is a devastating disease. This study will test whether a adenovirus based vaccine followed by a DNA plasmid administered via electrogenetransfer can elicit anti-tumor immunity and increase survival times. The vaccine will be an additional therapy to standard of care treatment. In people, Her2/neu has been expressed in this cancer and is associated with a poor prognosis. In unpublished canine testing, HER2/neu has been expressed and opens a therapeutic target against this cancer. Int Urol Nephrol. 2014 Nov 11. "Epub ahead of print" Prognostic role of HER2 expression in bladder cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Zhao J1, Xu W, Zhang Z, Song R, Zeng S, Sun Y, Xu C. The vaccine targets this Her2/neu pathway of tumorigenesis allowing the body's immune system to battle the cancer in addition to standard therapies. PROCEDURE: Currently, the vaccine is a series of 5 treatments (2 adenovirus/Her2/neu) followed by 3 DNA/plasmid administered via electrogenetherapy (EGT). Each is administered every 2 weeks and there is an option for continued monthly boosters for those patients maintaining remission. The first two (2) adenovirus vaccines (prime) are administered via simple intra-muscular injection. The last three (3) of the series (boosters) are administered under a short anesthesia via EGT. No placebos are involved and the study is unfunded and follows USDA regulations. This immunotherapy is an extension of the center's telomerase cancer vaccine that has shown success against canine lymphoma in Europe. There is no guarantee and some patients may not benefit. Our group recently published on this: Overexpression of HER-2 via immunohistochemistry in canine urinary bladder transitional cell carcinoma - A marker of malignancy and possible therapeutic target.Millanta F,ImpellizeriJ, McSherry L, Rocchigiani G, Aurisicchio L, Lubas G.Vet Comp Oncol. 2017 Sep 4. doi: 10.1111/vco.12345. If you are interested in this clinical trial, please go to our website http://www.petcancerinformation.com and have your veterinarian fill out our referral form. Please fax or email this along with pertinent lab results. Most patients are candidates, however a formal phone consult will determine options. Thank you for your interest.

rows.title: MRI-guided treatment for gliomas in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose This study will evaluate the safety and feasibility of MRI-guided High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation (HFIRE) for the treatment of brain cancers and aim to optimize the technology to achieve tumor destruction of multiple brain tumor types. Background HFIRE is a newer generation technology, similar to the NanoKnife system which is in clincial trial in humans for the destruction soft tissues (i.e. tumors or cancers) via irreversible electroporation (IRE). We have previously demonstrated the safety of IRE for the treatment of canine brain tumors and have safely performed HFIRE on soft-tissue tumors, including brian tumors, in client-owned dogs, cats, and horses. By placing thin electrodes within tissue, IRE uses electrical pulses to destroy tissues by disrupting cellular membranes. The IRE method is less invasive and disruptive than traditional methods of surgical tumor resection. HFIRE offers additional advantages over traditional IRE in that the high-frequency pulses do not result in electrically induced muscular contractions, eliminating the need for more anesthesic agents, and offering the potential to selectively kill cancer cells and spare normal, healthy cells based on the physical characteristics of the cells. Therefore, HFIRE is ideally suited to the treatment of cancers in anatomically sensitive areas, such as the brain. Our newest generation of HFIRE technology allows the neurosurgeon to perform the HFIRE treatment while the patient is in the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, which should improve the safety and efficacy of the procedure. Eligibility MRI evidence of a solitary mass lesion (consistent with glioma or meningioma) in the cerebrum that is at least 10 mm in diameter. Dogs with tumors previously treated with surgery are also eligible if there is MRI documented evidence of tumor progression. Clinical signs of mild to moderate neurologic dysfunction referable to the brain (Karnofsky Performance Score >70). No clinical or other diagnostic evidence of other significant systemic disease. Exclusion Criteria Dogs that are pregnant Uncontrolled seizures or other severe neurological signs Bone marrow suppression, or significant kidney or liver dysfunction evident on blood tests Concurrent infections or malignancy Prior treatment of the tumor with radiation therapy of any kind Study Design The HFIRE electrodes will be inserted into the brain tumor with MRI guidance and HFIRE pulses delivered using a treatment plan customized for each patient. Dogs will be cared for post-operatively using standard-of-care procedures for brain tumor patients, and monitored daily in the ICU for adverse events until discharge from the hospital. Following discharge, clinical follow-up examinations will be recommended and continued to be performed off-study according to standards of care for each patients specific type of tumor. Compensation The fees associated with the HFIRE treatment and the associated pre- and post-operative hospitalization costs will be covered by the study sponsor. An additional follow-up clinical visit and brain MRI examination 6-8 weeks after the surgery to evaluate the treatment will also be covered by the study.

rows.description: This clinical trial, led by the National Cancer Institute and Vyriad, Inc., assesses the safety and effectiveness of a cancer-killing virus (VSV-IFN-NIS) when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in mice, normal dogs, and in a small study of pet dogs with cancer have shown the virus to be safe at certain doses. This virus is currently being evaluated in human patients with liver cancer in an FDA-approved trial. Results of this study will be used to help design future clinical trials evaluating VSV-IFN-NIS in dogs with relapsed or refractory cancer. Principal Investigator at the University of Minnesota: Mike Henson, DVM, PhD, DACVIM. Eligible dogs must: - have a malignant tumor that is accessible and large enough (>1 inch in most cases) to allow samples to be collected from it for analysis (biopsies) - tumors can be either newly diagnosed or recurrent and of almost any type except mast cell tumors or hemangiosarcoma - weigh 20 kg or more (44 lbs) be feeling well with no significant health concerns, other than the malignancy, identified on routine diagnostic testing (blood and urine tests, x-rays, ultrasound) - be up to date on vaccines, flea/tick prevention and internal parasite control - not be in contact with livestock - have stopped any drug therapies for the cancer at least two weeks prior to enrollment - have stopped any radiation therapy for the tumor at least six weeks prior to enrollment Other restrictions may apply, call for details. Other restrictions may apply, call for details. Study summary: A screening visit to determine eligibility to include physical exam, history, bloodwork, chest x-rays, possible abdominal ultrasound. First day of the study (Mondays): pre-treatment physical exam, tumor measurements, blood samples, lymph node aspirates, tumor biopsies. Second day (Tuesday): Virus administration intravenously, monitoring, blood, urine, fecal and saliva sampling. Depending on the group to which a dog is assigned, a 2nd intravenous dose of virus may be given on the second day. Dogs must remain in the VMC until Friday for monitoring and sampling. Follow-up visits are necessary the VMC on Day 8, Day 15, Day 22, and Day 29 to measure tumor response and collect samples (e.g. blood, urine, saliva, feces). Dogs will be anesthetized for collection of biopsy samples prior to treatment and on Day 3, Day 8 and Day 29. Please contact Andrea Eckert, CVT for more information or to inquire about enrolling in this study.

rows.description: Progress has been slow to improve therapies and outcomes for dogs diagnosed with a very common tumor - lymphoma. To accelerate our understanding of this cancer in dogs and identify novel treatments to improve survival, we are collecting a sample of lymph node tissue from dogs diagnosed with lymphoma that have not yet begun therapy for their cancer. The tissue collected will be used to identify ways to improve disease detection, prognosis, and treatment options for dogs with multicentric lymphoma. The project is part of theCornell Lymphoma Programand involves researchers across the Cornell Ithaca campus and at Weill Cornell in New York City. Your only commitment is to bring your dog forhis/her initial evaluation, diagnostic tests, and lymph node removal. We would also like to contact you and/or your veterinarian in the future to obtain follow-up information about your dog. Total expectation for hospitalization for diagnostic tests and surgery is two days.

rows.description: The goal of this study is to determine a safe dosage of a re-purposed antibiotic to use in dogs with lymphoma. This antibiotic may affect cancer cells through a variety of mechanisms and the most appropriate dosage to use in dogs with cancer is unknown. Certain high dosages used to treat infections are associated with a high incidence of liver toxicity in dogs with lymphoma. This study evaluates the safety and tolerability of a lower dosage. The initial appointment will include the physical examination to determine eligibility and diagnostics that include blood work, x-rays of the chest, ultrasound of the abdomen, and dispensing of the medications. Owners must be willing to give their dog the medication orally twice daily at home and return to the hospital for recheck visits (5-6 visits over 1 month).

rows.title: Anti-cancer vaccine (MediVet Biologics K9-ACV) for dogs with any malignant tumor
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Purpose and Brief Study Description: If enrolled into this study, your dogs own tumor will be used to generate a very specific anti-cancer vaccine. Cancer vaccines represent a form of active immunotherapy, whereby they exert an antitumor effect by engaging the host immune response. Additional advantages of cancer vaccines are exquisite specificity, low toxicity, and the potential for a durable therapeutic effect / benefit as a result of the induction of immunologic memory. Autologous cancer vaccines, such as the K9-ACV (MediVet Biologics) utilized in this proposed project, are polyvalent therapeutic vaccines derived from whole tumor cells. Such vaccines are formulated on an individual case basis using tumor tissue biopsy samples from the actual patient. The vaccine system being employed in this project was developed by researchers at the University Of Kentucky College Of Medicine, in conjunction with MediVet Biologics, and was modeled on a vaccine system previously developed by the same research group at the University of Kentucky and investigated in human lung cancer patients. Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of a newly formulated anti-cancer vaccine (K9-ACV, MediVet Biologics) in dogs diagnosed with a spectrum of naturally-occurring cancers. We will be measuring the patients' systemic immunologic anti-tumor response to the vaccine. It is hypothesized that this vaccine will elicit an antitumor immunologic response resulting in improved disease-free intervals and median survival times in dogs with various tumor types without compromising quality of life. What does enrollment into this trial involve? After your dog is enrolled into this study, surgery will occur atVHC to remove ordebulk the primarytumor. Part of the tumor tissue will be submitted for histopathologic diagnosis, grading and surgical margin assessment, and the remainder (minimum 5g) for vaccine formulation by the team at the University of Kentucky/MediVet Biologics. While the vaccination series cannot start until 7-14 days after the initial surgery, as this is how long the vaccine formulation takes, approval of enrollment, accompanied by owner informed consent, is required prior to surgery. In all cases of enrolled dogs, the surgical procedure to be performed would be considered standard of care treatment of that particular tumor type. Following surgery, enrolled dogs will be placed into one of two treatment groups at the owners request; the first receiving simply the vaccination series, and the second receiving the vaccination series in combination with the appropriate standard of care chemotherapy.If post-operative chemotherapy is elected by the owners, it will be performed by VHC Oncology Service. Recheck exams and blood work are required for monitoring of the patients immune response to the vaccine, as well as periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound. All study activities must occur at the VHC. Client Compensation: This study covers the cost of vaccine formulation and administration, as well as recheck exams and blood work for enrolled dogs. Periodic monitoring chest x-rays and ultrasound are also covered by the study for up to one year. Owner is responsible for the cost associated with pre-enrollment work-up and staging, which includes chest x-rays, abdominal ultrasound, blood work and urinalysis. In addition, the owner is responsible for the cost of surgery to remove or debulk the tumor.

rows.title: Canine brain tumor vaccine clinical trial
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Canine Brain Tumor Vaccine Clinical Trial We greatly appreciate your interest in our clinical study evaluating the use of a vaccine in dogs with brain tumors, specifically glioma. Your pets clinician will explain the disease characteristics of glioma as well as available treatment options. If you choose to participate in this clinical study, this handout will provide you with some insight into the purpose of this study and will explain your responsibilities and patient procedures. What are clinical trials? Clinical trials are research studies. They are used in all specialties of medicine to evaluate new types of treatment. Clinical trials may be designed to determine the anti-cancer effects and side effects of new drugs, new surgical procedures, new radiation therapy procedures, or novel approaches to treatment (such as gene therapy or immunotherapy). Your pets clinician will discuss standard treatment and clinical trial options with you. It is your decision whether or not you want your pet to participate in a clinical trial. You may discuss your pets participation with your family and your pets veterinarian. If you have any questions, please ask your pets clinician for additional information. Why is this clinical trial being conducted? Gliomas in dogs are known to be a very aggressive cancer with relatively short survival times despite our best efforts at treatment. Because of this, we are always looking for new ways to treat this disease. Many new cancer treatments are aimed at activating the patients own immune system (called immunotherapy) to potentially make it more effective at fighting off the cancer. One form of immunotherapy is tumor vaccines. This vaccine was developed in the Dow Laboratory, and targets the cancer stem cells, which are the precursor cells that then migrate and mature into active tumor cells with appropriate biochemical signals. These cancer stem cells are thought to be responsible for the inevitable recurrence of gliomas. These cells are present in the subventricular zone of the brain, and as such are not accessible for resection with the primary tumor. As these precursor cells are not in active division and thus are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation therapy, immunotherapies are likely the key to achieving improved outcomes for gliomas. A successful vaccine that targets these cancer stem cells would be invaluable. The goal of this study is to evaluate preliminary tumor response to vaccination as well as vaccine tolerability. Which patients are eligible to participate in this clinical trial? To be eligible for this study, dogs must have a brain tumor that is presumed to be in the glioma family based on MRI characteristics. They must also have sufficiently stable clinical signs to allow likely survival of at least one month. The patients neurological status must be such that he/she is strongly ambulatory without assistance, and that seizures (if occurring) are controlled with anti-convulsant medication. Dogs must not be receiving prednisone, or must be on a dose <0.5 mg/kg/day for at least 72 hours prior to starting the vaccine series, and maintain below that threshold for at least 7 days post-final vaccine. Past radiation therapy patients and chemotherapy patients are not eligible. Dogs with preexisting allergic airway disease or low heart rate may not receive propranolol, which is one of two medications given in addition to the vaccine to enhance the vaccine effect, and may be excluded at the investigator's discretion. Dogs must undergo some diagnostic testing at CSU prior to starting the vaccines to ensure that they are eligible, including complete blood count, chemistry profile, urinalysis, and needle biopsy (not debulking) of the tumor (costs will be covered by the study). What will happen if my pet participates in this clinical trial? If enrolled, dogs will first have a needle biopsy of their tumor, and if confirmed glioma, then they will receive a vaccine under the skin once every other week for a total 6 vaccines, followed by once monthly vaccine boosters. Serial neurological exams will be performed at each visit during the study period, and recheck MRI scans of the brain will be done every 3 months after the first vaccine. Additional blood samples will be collected for study purposes prior to the first vaccine and then serially throughout the study to assess antitumor immune response. In addition to the vaccine, two additional medications (losartan and propranolol) will be given orally (by mouth) to enhance the effect of the vaccine. Once your pet has died or been euthanized, a post-mortem exam will be required for additional characterization of tumor type, growth, and cellular markers. What side effects or risks may my pet experience while participating in this clinical trial? Your pet may experience side effects. Possible side effects associated with the vaccine treatment include: Local vaccine site reactions (swelling, pain, redness, itching) Fever, mild loss of appetite, and/or lethargy for first 24 hours after vaccine injection Risk of anaphylaxis (rare) Cerebral edema and worsening of neurological signs (unlikely) due to peritumoral inflammation from exuberant response of tumor to vaccine Losartan may cause low blood pressure or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be decreased Propanolol may cause slow heart rate, low blood pressure, or lethargy; if this occurs the dosage will be adjusted Needle biopsy side effects may include: transient neurological decline, hemorrhage, infection, or less commonly permanent neurological decline or death The study is able to cover up to $500 in treatment costs for vaccine-associated adverse events if they occur. Adverse events are not anticipated, and most likely would involve simple local reactions that would require only oral medications to treat. Your pets clinician will discuss possible side effects with you and help you manage them if they occur. If your pet experiences anything unusual during the clinical trial, please contact your clinician. How long will my pet be in the clinical trial? The study period is 1 year. However, the length of your pets participation will depend on his/her response to the treatment. If your pets clinical signs are worsening or there is concern for tumor progression, your pet may be withdrawn from the study before it is completed. Your pets clinician will discuss continued treatment and diagnostic testing once the trial has ended. Can my pet withdraw from the clinical trial? You may decide to withdraw your pet from the clinical trial at any time. Tell your pets clinician if you are considering withdrawing your pet. It is important to discuss withdrawal in order to determine a plan for continued treatment of your pets cancer. Your clinician may stop your pet from continued participation in the clinical trial at any time if he/she believes it is in your pets best interest or if the trial is discontinued or if the trial protocol is not followed. What financial incentives will CSU provide for my pets participation? All required study activities once enrolled (not including the diagnostic tests to determine eligibility), will be performed at no cost. (Costs for medications or treatments that are not included as part of the study, are not covered by the study). There is no charge for the postmortem examination. In addition, up to $500 will be available for treatment of vaccine-related adverse events. What are my responsibilities during the clinical trial? You are responsible for the costs of any elective services, medications, or additional hospitalization fees not required by the study. In addition, any costs for treatment of adverse events beyond the $500 covered by the study will be your financial responsibility, as well as the cost and any other tests recommended by your pets neurologist that are not a required component of the study. You are expected to make and keep all appointments, according to the clinical trial protocol. Questions? Please do not hesitate to obtain additional information from your pets neurology clinician if you do not understand something about the study or your pets care and treatment. CSU Principal Investigator: Dr. Rebecca Packer, (970) 297-4543, email: Rebecca.Packer@colostate.edu Emergency Assistance: CSU VTH, (970) 297-5000. 2008, Animal Cancer Center, Colorado State University

rows.title: Validation of a novel imaging device to detect cancerous vs normal cells during brain tumor resection
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Which dogs can participate in this study? In this study, dogs that have been diagnosed with a surgically resectable brain tumor, based on MRI, are eligible for the study. Study Activities In this study, surgery would proceed according to normal standard of care; however, during surgery a novel imaging device will be used to record the chemical signal of the tissues visible during surgery. This imaging device is completely noninvasive, and will allow us to learn the differences in chemical signal of normal brain tissue compared to tumor tissue. This is important because visually some brain tumors look identical to tumor tissue, so improved methods of recognizing abnormal cells during surgery are vital to improving surgical accuracy. The readings obtained during surgery will be compared to the biopsy samples obtained as a normal component of tumor resection. This study only requires noninvasive acquisition of biochemical recordings during surgery. The surgery itself is performed in the same manner as any standard surgical resection of your pet's brain tumor. Financial Incentives This study does not include administration of novel therapies; however, it does offer a $5000 subsidy towards the cost of surgical resection. Please note that specific estimates for the remaining out-of-pocket surgical expenses can be provided upon request based on your pet's tumor location, neurological status, and specific surgical approach required.

rows.title: COTC021: Evaluation of Orally Administered mTOR Inhibitor Rapamycin in Dogs in the Adjuvant Setting with Osteosarcoma; COTC022: A
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: This clinical trial led by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) and sponsored by the Morris Animal Foundation seeks to evaluate in dogs with osteosarcoma the safety and effectiveness of Standard of Care therapy, with or without adjuvant rapamycin administration. Standard of Care is defined as definitive surgery, being amputation of the affected limb, followed by 4 doses of intravenous carboplatin chemotherapy given on a q21 day schedule. Carboplatin has been safely and effectively used to treat appendicular osteosarcoma in dogs for > 20 years, but the potential for unforeseen potentially life-threatening side effects from surgery, chemotherapy, and/or progressive cancer does exist. ALL dogs enrolled onto study will receive Standard of Care therapy; however, through a randomization process, some dogs entered into study will also receive additional therapy with oral rapamycin. Rapamycin is a drug currently approved for immunosuppression during preparatory and maintenance regimens for organ and bone marrow transplant in human patients. Early work with rapamycin suggests that this agent might also have anti-cancer properties by inhibiting (reducing the effects of) an important pathway in cancer progression known as mTOR. Preclinical studies of rapamycin in mice, as well as recent data using analogous drugs in human patients (rapalogs), suggest that mTOR blockade might be effective in the treatment of several cancers. Studies in mice have shown rapamycin to be safe when used to treat experimental cancers. In a recently completed study of rapamycin in dogs with cancer, a dose and schedule for rapamycin administration have been defined which appears to be safe and tolerable by most dogs. These 2 studies (COTC021 and COTC022) will evaluate if orally administered rapamycin following Standard of Care improves long-term disease control.

rows.title: VIGOR Trial
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA), the most common bone tumor found in the dog, has already spread by the time we diagnose 90% of the cases. Survival times are limited, from 3-4 months with surgery alone, and 9-14 months with the addition of chemotherapy. In order to improve survival in dogs, newer therapies are needed. We are studying genetically modified Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV-IFN-NIS) which has been shown to be effective against cancer in the laboratory and in a pilot study of eight dogs. The study will treat dogs with VSV intravenously, followed by amputation of the affected limb 10 days later, then followed by chemotherapy with carboplatin. February 2018: expanded trial to placebo-controlled. Dogs will be screened for acceptability, including a CT scan under anesthesia. Once enrolled, dogs typically spend the week at the Veterinary Medical Center (VMC). We will perform a tumor biopsy under anesthesia and take baseline samples of blood, cheek, urine and stool on Monday. On Tuesday dogs receive the treatment with VSV-IFN-NIS or saline placebo and will be housed in isolation, closely monitored by our team, for a period of time (6-24 hrs). We will sample blood, cheek, urine and stool periodically to detect virus shedding and immune responses. On Wed - Fri, we will monitor the dog and take additional samples. Dogs go home on Friday. Recheck visits are weekly for 1st month. Day 10 is the amputation surgery. Chemotherapy begins about Day 21, and will continue for six treatments (standard protocol through the Oncology Service). Study rechecks are at months 3, 6, and one year. We will repeat a CT scan typically at the 3 month visit.

rows.title: Evaluation of Fasting in Mitigation of Vincristine and Carboplatin Chemotherapy Associated Side Effects in Cancer-Bearing Dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Vincristine and carboplatin are two commonly used chemotherapeutics in veterinary and human medicine. Patients with lymphoma, osteosarcoma and a range of other malignancies may be treated with these drugs. Unfortunately, adverse events such as lethargy, vomiting, diarrhea or reduction in blood cell counts may occur in dogs administered vincristine or carboplatin. The objectives of this study are to determine the effect of short-term fasting on the incidence and severity of adverse events (toxicity) in dogs treated with vincristine or carboplatin, and to identify the effect of fasting on serum glucose, insulin and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) concentration. This trial protocol will follow standard of care therapy aside from patient fasting and blood collection for serum glucose, insulin and IGF-1 concentration. Based on randomization, enrolled dogs will be fasted for 24 hours prior to their first or second dose of chemotherapy (carboplatin or vincristine). Dogs will be fed normally prior to the other scheduled chemotherapy treatment. Enrollment: dogs will need a physical exam (PE), complete blood count (CBC), serum biochemistry (Chem), and urinalysis (UA) within 2-7 days of the first chemotherapy treatment. Dogs will either be in the vincristine or carboplatin treatment group based on their treatment plan and disease process.

rows.title: The treatment of canine brain tumors with Temozolomide incorporated into poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) microcylinders
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Many brain cancers are not accessible to surgical excision, and use of chemotherapy drugs is limited by the blood brain barrier. In an effort to deliver chemotherapy drugs directly into a cancer, novel polymeric microcylinders have been developed using poly (lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) as a biocompatible drug delivery system. These novel microcylinders have been designed to be amenable to stereotactic implantation, allowing for a minimally-invasive implantation procedure. The polymer can be adjusted for various degradation times, allowing the associated drug to be delivered over a prescribed period of time. Because the drug can be placed directly into the cancerous tissue, the blood brain barrier is bypassed entirely. This enables a high dosage of chemotherapy to be delivered into the cancer without the risk of systemic side effects associated with high-dose chemotherapy including myelosuppression or gastrointestinal upset. Temozolamide is a chemotherapy drug that has been FDA approved for the treatment of glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) in humans, and was shown to provide a statistically significant benefit to 2-year survival and progression-free survival time in humans as part of multimodal therapy for GBM. Temozolomide has been demonstrated as safe in dogs with lymphoma, but there have been no studies evaluating its clinical efficacy for any type of brain tumor in dogs. The current objective is to study implantation of temozolomide and gadolinium-infused PLGA microcylinders in dogs with gliomas. Our preliminary studies confirm that PLGA microcylinders infused with both temozolomide and gadolinium are clinically well-tolerated in healthy dogs.

rows.title: Novel gene therapy for the treatment of canine brain tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: This project is a collaborative effort between Celsion, Corporation and veterinarians at Veterinary Referral & Critical Care (VRCC) of Manakin-Sabot, VA evaluating a novel gene therapy (GEN-1) for the treatment of brain tumors. The goal of this project is to evaluate the safety and feasibility of intra-cranially administering GEN-1 following tumor resection surgery. The results of this study will be used to support the initiation of clinical trials aimed at treating human patients with glioblastoma multiforme. The following treatment design will be used: Surgery to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Subcutaneous implantation of a reservoir device with access to the resection cavity Repeated administration (3x) of the gene therapy (GEN-1) through the device directly into the resection cavity. What dogs are eligible for the project? Any dog that is approximately 10 Kg in weight or greater with an intra-axial brain tumor and that is healthy enough to undergo resection surgery can be included in this study. The specific tumor type will not be an eligibility requirement although there will be requirements regarding the location of the tumor that will inform a final eligibility decision. How much does it cost? All project related treatments, analytical work and followup will be performed at no cost to the dog's owners. Owners will be responsible for transportation to and from VRCC for treatments and follow-up visits. What is the therapy? In this study, GEN-1, a nanoparticle formulation that contains the IL-12 gene will be repeatedly delivered intra-cranially into dogs following tumor resection surgery. IL-12 protein is known to have very potent anti-tumor properties that work by stimulating the bodys own immune response to help kill tumor cells. In addition, IL-12 can also help to prevent the formation of new blood vessels that are required for tumor growth. Use of GEN-1 is currently being evaluated in human clinical trials for treating ovarian cancer and has shown in animal models that it can slow and/or eliminate a wide variety of tumor types, including glioblastomas. Although this study is designed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of repeatedly administering GEN-1 into the resection cavity in the brain that has resulted from surgically removing a brain tumor, it has the potential to reduce or eradicate the remaining tumor in dogs suffering from brain cancer. Please contact Dr. Jeff Clarke, DVM, DACVIM or Dr. Anna Aman, DVM, DACVS at VRCC for more information. rows.description: Cancer stem cells (CSC) are now considered a primary driver of tumor recurrence following chemotherapy or radiation therapy, as well as a driver of cancer metastasis. There currently are no therapeutics that can selectively target CSC for elimination. We hypothesize that it may be possible to target CSC for elimination by the immune system (T cells and antibodies specifically), using properly designed stem cell vaccines. The goal of this study is to determine if a new type of cancer vaccine targeting cancer stem cells can induce an immune response against the tumor and if the vaccine can slow tumor growth or induce tumor regression. A second goal of the study is to determine if vaccine responses can be enhanced by administration of two additional immune stimulating drugs. The first is losartan, a drug also used to treat high blood pressure, and the second is CLDC, a liposome immune stimulant that has been used previously in dogs, cats, and other species with cancer and as a general immune stimulant. Administration of the CLDC immune stimulant requires a second visit 24 hours after each vaccine in administered. Blood samples are collected for study purposes prior to starting vaccine treatment and at 1, 2, and 3 months of the study protocol. Standard bloodwork (CBC, chemistry profile) and urinalysis and chest x-rays are rechecked at 1, 2, and 3 months as well.
