rows.title: Novel limb sparing surgery using individualized 3D-printed implants in dogs
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Osteosarcoma is a tumor of bone. It destroys the bone it is originating from and causes pain. In treating dogs with this cancer, some form of therapy is typically directed at the tumor itself. It can be a limb amputation, radiation therapy, or limb sparing surgery. As the name implies, limb sparing surgery is a surgical procedure where the tumor is removed while preserving the function of the limb. For tumors that are located close to the wrist, many different techniques are possible but the risk of complication remains relatively high. The 3 main complications are infection, implant-related problems, and recurrence of the tumor in the limb. With currently-available techniques, the risk of an infection developing in the limb following limb sparing surgery can be as high as 75%, the risk of implant related problem as high as 60% and local recurrence is seen in 15%-25%. Many deficiencies exist with the currently available implants used for limb sparing in dogs. With the advent of 3D-printing, we have developed a process that allows us to manufacture an implant specifically designed for each individual dog that undergoes limb sparing. With these improved implants, we predict the risk of implant-related complications will significantly decrease and may also help decrease the risk of an infection. The goal of this clinical trial is to demonstrate that the process we have developed to create 3D-printed individualized implants is feasible in the clinical setting and can lead to a successful outcome for limb sparing in dogs.

rows.description: Doxorubicin-containing combination chemotherapy protocols are considered the standard of care for the treatment of canine lymphoma, the most common of which is CHOP, which includes the drugs cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. There are multiple versions of the CHOP protocol that vary the order of drugs given and the length of treatment. Despite numerous iterations of this protocol, outcomes tend to be similar among all of these protocols, with remission rates of > 90% and disease-free interval of approximately 9 months, with overall survival of about one year from the time of diagnosis. rows.title: Pharmacokinetic analysis of vinblastine in tumor bearing cats and analysis of population covariates
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Vinblastine has been used in feline cancer patients mostly as a component of multi-drug treatment protocols for lymphoma. Response rates, progression-free survival and lymphoma-specific survival are similar between cats receiving vinblastine or vincristine as part of a multi-drug protocol for lymphoma. However, cats receiving vinblastine may have a lower incidence of gastrointestinal toxicity, and this can be a deciding factor in choosing vinblastine over vincristine for treatment of lymphoma in cats. The incidence of neutropenia in cats following administered vinblastine versus vincristine does not appear to differ and dose reductions due to neutropenia are sometimes required during vinblastine therapy. No pharmacokinetic data exist for vinblastine in the cat. In other species, vinblastine demonstrates either a bi- or tri-exponential decline in plasma concentrations with abundant distribution to tissues that occurs rapidly after dosing. Vinblastine readily accumulates within the cellular component of blood, as it binds to tubulin within platelets and blood cells; up to 50% of drug may distribute to the cellular compartment of blood within 20 minutes of administration. Consistent with the findings of abundant tissue distribution, vinblastine has a large volume of distribution for and plasma protein binding values ranging from 43-99% depending on the species studied. Extensive hepatic metabolism of vinblastine leads to formation of one major metabolite, 4-desacetylvinblastine, suggested to have equal or greater antitumor activity to the parent molecule in dogs and humans. It is unknown if metabolism in cats also produces this active compound. Of note, pharmacokinetic studies in all other species have identified substantial inter- and intra-individual variability in pharmacokinetics which is noted clinically by the equally large variability in neutropenia following equivalent doses.It is important to understand the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in the population of patients that are receiving this drug; older, cancer-bearing cats that may have other co-morbid diseases that can affect pharmacokinetic profiles, i.e. hepatic or renal disease. Variability in pharmacokinetics is likely to be larger in this population when compared to younger, healthy cats. This study is designed to obtain the information required to describe the pharmacokinetics of vinblastine in cats and associate the variability in pharmacokinetic parameters with patient variables.

rows.title: Nasal Cancer Treatment with Electrochemotherapy
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description:
Nasal cancer in dogs and cats are uncommon with carcinomas being most common in dogs. Treatment has been limited to external beam radiation therapy at significant expense and often multiple days of anesthesia needed. Median survival is about 1 year and side effects are common. Electrochemotherapy is the use of electrical impulses to open cell membranes driving chemotherapy locally, i.e. a targeted therapy.


We now have an electrode that may be used for nasal tumors based on published material below:.


Radiol Oncol.2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430. doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec. Minimally InvasiveElectrochemotherapyProcedure for TreatingNasalDuct Tumors inDogs using a Single Needle Electrode. Maglietti F,Tellado M,Olaiz N,Michinski S,Marshall G


Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis.


The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure. Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure

PLX 4720 is closely related to vemurafenib (Zelboraf, PLX4032), another BRAF inhibitor approved for the treatment of human melanoma carrying activating mutations in BRAF. It was recently determined that approximately 80% of canine bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinomas-TCC) carry activating mutations in BRAF identical to those found in human melanoma. Unfortunately, vemurafenib has unfavorable oral bioavailability in dogs, necessitating the use of another analog with better pharmacokinetic properties. Recently, healthy volunteer client owned dogs were enrolled into a clinical trial to evaluate the pharmacokinetics of a single dose of PLX4720 given orally. This was well tolerated and provided critical data regarding expected pharmacokinetic variability and likely dosing necessary to reach biologically relevant blood levels of drug for the current clinical trial. Objective of the trial: To evaluate the biologic activity associated with oral administration of PLX4720 to dogs bladder cancer and with BRAF mutation, and to assess adverse events associated with chronic PLX4720 dosing. Eligible patients (any breed of dog) must meet all of the following criteria: Be greater than 1 year of age Weigh at least 5 kg Have a diagnosis of transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder with measurable disease Be medically healthy with no clinically significant physical findings Prior chemotherapy or radiation must be completed 2 weeks prior to study entry Be able to receive oral medication on a daily basis Urine must be positive for the BRAF mutation What does enrolling my dog in this clinical trial involve? All dogs will receive PLX4270 once per day, dogs will receive PLX4270 for 28 days at which time an assessment of response to therapy will be performed. rows.title: Prophylactic Total Lung Irradiation Combined with Standard of Care for Osteosarcoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Osteosarcoma (OSA) is the most common type of bone cancer in dogs, primarily occurring in the fore- and hindlimbs. It is an aggressive tumor with local bone destruction and severe pain where it originates and early metastasis (spread) to other sites within the body. The primary site of metastasis is to the lungs with >90% of dogs having at least microscopic metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, although surgical removal of the tumor via amputation of the affected limb provides palliation, these patients will eventually die from the development of multiple tumors within the lungs in only a few months. The addition of chemotherapy to address these secondary tumors increases survival over amputation alone and has been the accepted standard of care (SOC) for decades. However, the average survival still does not exceed a year and only a small percentage of dogs survive two years or longer. Thus, more effective treatment protocols are desperately needed. In human oncology, an approach that has been previously investigated is the delivery of low-dose radiation to the lungs (total lung irradiation; TLI) in the hopes of killing the microscopic cancer cells that are present. In these human studies, low-dose TLI, alone or combined with chemotherapy, was found to be safe but clinical benefit varied. Although safety data exists for TLI in healthy and tumor-bearing dogs, its effect on survival in dogs with OSA has been studied on a very limited and non-optimized basis and never in conjunction with SOC: amputation and chemotherapy. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate TLI plus SOC for dogs with OSA in a prospective clinical trial. After undergoing amputation (either here at NC State or at another institution) dogs will be enrolled and starting within 3 days following surgery will begin a protocol of 10 daily fractions of TLI followed by 6 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy (as per our protocol for the adjuvant treatment of canine OSA; may be performed here at NC State "preferred" or with another veterinarian if the clients cannot pursue chemotherapy here). Following completion of the carboplatin protocol dogs will then be monitored with serial thoracic radiographs performed every 2 months (our standard practice) to assess for metastatic disease and any potential adverse effects of TLI. Our primary objective is to evaluate the effect of adding TLI to SOC on metastasis-free interval (MFI; the time from amputation to development of the aforementioned lung nodules or spread elsewhere, e.g. bone) and overall survival time (ST; the time from amputation to death or euthanasia). Our secondary objective is to obtain short- and long-term safety data by using serial bloodwork, chest x-rays, and respiratory (client-provided history, physical exam) assessments. We hypothesize that the addition of TLI will significantly improve patient outcome and will be well-tolerated with minimal to no hematologic or respiratory toxicity.

The drug papaverine has been given to humans for over 100 years with an excellent safety profile. Researchers at Ohio State have identified an unknown effect of papaverine that reduces oxygen consumption in tumor cells. Studies in rodent tumors have shown that the effect of papaverine on reducing oxygen consumption reduces hypoxia and increases the effectiveness of radiation therapy.We are now asking if papaverine can reduce hypoxia in canine sarcoma. The current study will be an addition to the regular treatment of your dog's tumor, and will not affect how that therapy is given. What qualifies my pet for this trial? To be included in the trial, dogs must fulfill the following criteria: 1.Body weight of at least 5 lbs or 2.27 kg 2.Adequate organ function as indicated by standard laboratory tests 3.Skin or subcutaneous soft tissue sarcoma as diagnosed by cytology or histopathology. Tumor can be new or recurrent. 4.Minimum tumor size of 2cm diameter. 5.Able to undergo general anesthesia and surgery for treatment of soft tissue sarcoma Exclusion Criteria Dogs with the following criteria or conditions will be excluded from the study: 1.Evidence of underling disease conditions such as clinically significant abnormalities in their labwork that would indicate renal, cardiac, or hepatic dysfunction. 2.Result of diagnostic testing (cytology and/or histopathology) are not clearly documented. 3.History of prior radiation therapy to tumor. Prescreening (Day -3 to -7): Pre-Treatment Diagnostics and ScreeningAfter signature of Owner Informed Consent, the dog will have a medical history completed and undergo a physical examination. Blood and urine samples will be collected and submitted for complete blood count (CBC), serum chemistry panel, and urinalysis. Prior to general anesthesia, the patient will have been fasted 10 hours before admission or overnight during hospitalization but can receive water ad libitum until the morning of the planned general anesthesia. The dog will be premedicated using a protocol developed by the board-certified anesthesiologist. The dog will have an MRI of the tumor. Following completion of MRI the dog will have papaverine administered IV and be monitored. General anesthesia will be maintained and sixty minutes following completion of papaverine administration the dog will be transported back and have a repeat MRI of the tumor. rows.description: Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs. Recent studies indicate that certain immune cells such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes play an important role in tumor metastasis in diseases such as osteosarcoma. Certain anti-tumor drugs, such as toceranib, have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. The drugs losartan and propranolol have both been shown to modify the tumor microenvironment and reduce immune suppression caused by the tumor. The goal of this study is to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of a 3-drug combination of toceranib, losartan, and propranolol in dogs with metastatic osteosarcoma. The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. Both diseases can cause diarrhea, vomiting, pain, and malabsorption of food. However, recent data indicate that those two conditions may represent a continuum, and more studies are necessary to better understand the conditions. Since the diseases are similar and the symptoms overlap and are nonspecific, diagnosis can be challenging, and may require expensive and invasive procedures. In addition, although the general treatment for both conditions is similar, treatment may mask more aggressive and potentially costly diseases. Thus, developing better diagnostic approaches is essential to provide better care to feline patients. Dogs with documented progressive disease (increase in size of either the primary tumor or metastatic lesions) will undergo re-evaluation 2 weeks later to confirm disease progression and not pseudoprogression. Overall tolerability and biological activity will be based on clinical and pharmacodynamic endpoints.

rows.title: Fully Canine Anti-PD1 for Urothelial Carcinoma in Dogs: Safety and Tolerability
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common type of bladder cancer to affect dogs. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, with the aim being to reduce the size of the tumor, alleviate symptoms, and improve the dog's quality of life. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment approach for many types of cancer, including canine urothelial carcinoma. Immunotherapies aim to harness the body's immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. They can be particularly attractive for treating cancers that are difficult to access surgically or that have metastasized (spread to other parts of the body).This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy when used in dogs with urothelial carcinoma. The therapy specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells, which usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells. Immunotherapies that are able to inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively.Urothelial carcinoma in dogs shares many biological and molecular features with human urothelial carcinoma, including their ability to be shielded from the immune system. Human clinical trials in urothelial carcinoma investigating similar immunotherapies have shown these therapies to be more effective than traditional chemotherapies in some cases. Development of an immunotherapy that is safe and beneficial in canine urothelial carcinoma patients will advance veterinarians ability to treat this disease and will provide an important model to inform future canine and human clinical trials in this area. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.

rows.title: Flourescence Lifetime Imaging for real time surgical guidance in oral tumors
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: The goal of oral cancer surgery is to remove all cancer cells to prevent local recurrence and distant spread to other organs. However, there is currently no pre-operative or intraoperative diagnostic test that is capable of accurately identifying all cancer cells, especially at the leading tumor edge where there is only microscopic disease. Thus, to ensure no cancer cells are left behind, a border of grossly normal appearing tissue (up to 2 cm) is also removed during surgery. Yet, in the oral cavity, removal of bordering healthy tissue is typically associated with severe structural, functional and cosmetic side effects. Most notably, the ability to eat may be compromised. There is an urgent need for intraoperative diagnostic tests that can delineate healthy from cancer tissue in real-time. The aim of this study is to evaluate the use of florescence lifetime imaging with Protophoryin IX (a natural intermediate in the iron pathway that fluoresces under blue light) to accurately diagnose cancer versus normal tissue during surgery. We will also characterize the tissue changes that drive differences in florescence emission between the tumor, peritumoral region (area of potential pre-malignant cells), and healthy tissue with spatial transcriptomics. This will allow us to also create biomarkers for early diagnosis of cancer and decide when florescence imaging is most likely to be helpful. If successful, the use of florescence lifetime imaging with PpIX during surgery would ensure the surgeon successfully removes all cancer cells while simultaneously sparing normal healthy tissue.

rows.title: Lattice radiation therapy’s effect on the immune response in canine sinonasal carcinoma
rows.discovery_method: Actual official public gallery pagination;853unique records
rows.description: Sinonasal cancer is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed progress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to evaluate a new radiation treatment known as Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT). A current method of radiation therapy used to treat canine sinonasal carcinoma (SC), called stereotactic body radiotherapy therapy (SBRT), distributes a high dose of radiation uniformly across the tumor. Lattice radiation therapy (LRT) differs from SBRT in that instead of administering that uniform high dose of radiation throughout the tumor, several small spheres of high dose radiation are administered within the tumor and the rest of the tumor receives a lower dose of radiation. LRT has shown promise in early studies to provide tumor control with low normal tissue toxicity, suspected to be due to improved blood flow and immune responses compared to uniform, high dose radiation therapy. Our goal is to look at the differences in the tumors immune response during and after treatment as well as the clinical response with LRT compared to our standard SBRT. Dogs enrolled into this study will be treated with LRT. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush under anesthesia. The following procedures will be performed in all dogs enrolled in the study: CT scan for radiation therapy planning Lattice radiation therapy; 3 treatments given once daily over consecutive business days under general anesthesia Nasal flush, 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Blood collection (9-19 mL), 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Tumor biopsy at the 2 week post-LRT time point under general anesthesia Recheck CT scan 3, 6, 12 months, and 18-months post-LRT under general anesthesia.
